title: Inside Lagos Fashion Week: ten collections that set the tone for 2027
excerpt: From hand-woven aso-oke tailoring to recycled denim, the week showed a generation of designers who build locally and sell globally.

children.text: By the fourth night, the most telling detail was not on the runway. It was in the front row, where buyers from Johannesburg and Milan sat beside tailors from Oshodi, all of them leaning forward at the same moment whenever a jacket came out in hand-woven cloth. The week felt less like a showcase and more like a trade fair that had learned how to dress up.

The common thread was production. Almost every designer we spoke to backstage could name the town their fabric came from and the person who wove, dyed or cut it. That used to be a talking point, something printed on a press release. This season it was simply how the clothes were made, and it showed in the finish: hems that sat flat, linings that were not an afterthought, buttons sourced from the same place as the cloth.

body.caption: A finale walk of aso-oke suiting, shot from the end of the runway on night three.
body.alt: A finale walk of aso-oke suiting, shot from the end of the runway on night three.

children.text: The ten we keep thinking about
Ọ̀nà Atelier: aso-oke woven narrow and cut into double-breasted suits, with the selvedge left raw at the cuffs.
Kanu Kanu: recycled denim patched into long coats, the seams picked out in orange thread.
House of Ebube: column dresses in Akwete cloth, so simple they looked expensive.
Studio Ríbì: knitwear made with a cooperative in Ilorin, in the colours of a kola nut.
Maison Ekanem: Efik wrapper skirts reworked as trousers, belted with brass.
Dọ̀dọ̀ Club: menswear for heat, everything unlined and cut a size larger than you think.
Ayọ̀ Lagos: adire shirting in a pale, almost grey indigo.
Nnamdi Okafor-Reid: tailoring with sleeves that tie at the back like a buba.
Ìrìn: shoes stitched in Aba with soles cut from old tyres.
Halima Sule: kaftans in raw silk, embroidered by women in Zaria.

body.quote: We stopped asking whether Lagos could make it. The question now is how much, and how fast.
body.cite: Folake Adisa, buyer for a Lekki concept store

children.text: Not everything worked. A few collections leaned so hard on heritage that the clothes felt like costume, and the denim was more interesting as an idea than on the body. But the strongest work was quiet and well made, and it had a customer in mind who lives here. That customer, it turns out, is exactly who the rest of the world wants to dress like. Expect to see these names again in March, and expect the waiting lists to be longer.

title: Street style: what Yaba wore to the weekend markets
excerpt: Oversized agbada shirts, vintage football jerseys and a lot of beaded bags. Our photographers spent two Saturdays on the street.

children.text: Yaba on a Saturday morning runs on two clocks. The traders at Tejuosho have been open since six, hauling bales and sweeping their patch of pavement; the students and young designers who come to dig through the okrika arrive closer to eleven, coffee in hand, already dressed for whatever comes after. We stood at the corner by the bend for two weekends and photographed the second crowd.

body.caption: A cropped agbada shirt over cargo shorts, Herbert Macaulay Way, 11.40am.
body.alt: A cropped agbada shirt over cargo shorts, Herbert Macaulay Way, 11.40am.

children.text: Volume, but make it practical

The agbada shirt was everywhere: the generous drape of the full robe, cut off at the hip and worn open over a vest. Tomiwa, a second-year architecture student, had his made by a tailor in Sabo for ₦12,000. “It is my father’s silhouette,” he said, “but I can carry a backpack in it.” Football jerseys were the other constant, almost all of them vintage and almost all of them from clubs nobody wearing them supports. The appeal is the colour and the shine. One woman wore a 1990s goalkeeper shirt, the kind with a print that looks like a migraine, tucked into a long linen skirt. It should not have worked. It did.

body.quote: Everything I am wearing cost less than my bag, and my bag was ₦8,000.

children.text: If there was one accessory that defined the two Saturdays, it was the beaded bag: small, structured, often made by the wearer or a friend. We counted more than thirty in a single afternoon. Some were coral and gold in the old Edo style, others were neon plastic strung on fishing line, and one was shaped exactly like a Nokia phone. Several people told us they had learned to make them from the same online tutorial, posted by a woman in Benin City, and two of them were already selling their own.

What ties it all together is resourcefulness worn proudly. Very little we saw was new, and almost nothing was expensive. But nearly every outfit had been altered, combined or rethought in a way that made it belong to the person wearing it: a sleeve shortened, a collar removed, a skirt made from two wrappers. That, more than any single trend, is what Yaba does best, and it is why we will be back on that corner before the year is out.

title: Adire is having its biggest year yet
excerpt: Indigo resist-dye cloth from Abeokuta is appearing everywhere, from Paris runways to office wear. We traced it back to the dye pits.

children.text: At Itoku market in Abeokuta, the indigo is sold in two forms: as dried leaf balls the size of a fist, and as cloth that has already been through the pit. This year, the cloth is moving faster than anyone can remember. Traders say orders from Lagos tailors have doubled since January, and the lengths that used to sit folded on the back shelves are gone by noon. Adire has never really gone out of fashion here, but for a long time it lived in a particular box: Sunday wear, gifts for visiting relatives, the occasional statement shirt. What has changed is where it shows up. We have seen it this year as office trousers, as a bomber jacket lining, as a full wedding party in matching pale blue.

body.caption: Lengths of adire eleko drying on a line behind a compound in Itoku.
body.alt: Lengths of adire eleko drying on a line behind a compound in Itoku.

children.text: Back to the pits

Mama Ronke Odusote has dyed cloth in the same compound for thirty-one years. She keeps eight clay pots sunk into the ground, each at a different stage of fermentation, and she can tell by the smell which one is ready. Her daughter now handles the orders on WhatsApp; her grandson photographs every finished piece against the white wall of the house. On the morning we visited, there were eleven orders waiting, two of them from customers abroad who had never been to Abeokuta.

body.quote: Before, people wanted it bright and new. Now they ask me for the old patterns, the ones my mother did. They want to know the names.

children.text: Those names matter. Patterns like olokun, the goddess of the sea, or ibadandun, Ibadan is sweet, carry stories, and younger buyers have started asking for them by name. A few designers in Lagos now include the pattern name and the dyer’s name on the garment label, which the dyers we met were quietly delighted about.

Prices have risen with demand. A two-yard length of hand-tied adire that sold for around ₦9,000 last year now goes for ₦13,000 to ₦15,000, and hand-painted eleko work costs more. The dyers were not complaining. Their concern was the cheaper printed imitations arriving from abroad, which look the part from a distance but bleed blue the first time they meet water. Buy from the pits if you can, and ask who made it.

title: Why every Nigerian designer is talking about deadstock
excerpt: Leftover fabric from factories is becoming the most sought-after material in Lagos studios. Here is who is using it well.

children.text: Deadstock is the polite name for what is left over: the bolts a factory over-ordered, the colour a client rejected, the end of a roll too short for a production run. For years it was sold off by the kilo to whoever turned up at the warehouse in Ikeja with a bus. Now designers are queuing for it, and the warehouses have started keeping waiting lists. The appeal is partly cost and partly story. A metre of good cotton twill from a deadstock dealer can cost half what the same cloth costs new, and it comes with no minimum order. For a label making forty pieces, that is the difference between a collection and a sketchbook.

body.caption: Rolls of end-of-line shirting at a fabric dealer in Ikeja, sorted by weight rather than colour.
body.alt: Rolls of end-of-line shirting at a fabric dealer in Ikeja, sorted by weight rather than colour.

children.text: Who is doing it well

Chisom Eze of the label Remnant builds every collection backwards: she buys first, then designs around what she found. Last season that meant fourteen jackets in a heavy grey wool originally woven for school uniforms. “You cannot plan for the colour,” she told us. “You plan for the cloth.” Bayo Ilesanmi takes a different route. His shirts mix three or four deadstock fabrics in one garment, with collars, yokes and cuffs in contrasting stripes. Each piece is slightly different, and he numbers them by hand inside the placket.

body.quote: The limit is the design. When there are only eleven metres, you think very hard about every cut.

children.text: There is a catch. Deadstock is finite by definition, which makes it difficult to restock a best-seller, and customers who missed a drop do not always understand why it cannot simply be made again. It can also be hard to know what you are buying: labels go missing, and fibre content is sometimes a guess. Several designers now burn-test a thread from every roll before they pay. And as demand rises, prices are creeping up. One dealer told us he has raised his rates twice since March, and that a buyer from Accra now visits every month.
Still, the shift feels real. When the most interesting clothes in a city are being made from what other people threw away, it changes how everyone thinks about waste, and about what counts as new.

title: Street style: Abuja after Friday prayers
excerpt: Starched kaftans, embroidered caps and the city's sharpest sandals. We spent three Fridays outside the mosques of Wuse and Garki.

children.text: Between half past one and two on a Friday, Abuja changes colour. The streets around the mosques in Wuse and Garki fill with white, cream and pale blue, and for about forty minutes the city becomes the best-dressed place in the country. We went with a photographer on three consecutive Fridays, waited until prayers had finished, and asked permission before every frame. Most people said yes. Several asked us to wait while they straightened a cap.

body.caption: A starched white kaftan and a hand-embroidered zanna cap, Wuse Zone 5.
body.alt: A starched white kaftan and a hand-embroidered zanna cap, Wuse Zone 5.

children.text: The kaftan, perfected

The basic garment barely changes from man to man: a long kaftan, often over matching trousers. The differences are in the details. Embroidery around the neckline ranges from a single line of white thread to dense, raised panels that take a tailor two weeks. Starch is a matter of personal philosophy. Some prefer the cloth soft; others want it stiff enough to stand on its own. Musa, a civil engineer, told us his tailor in Kubwa has made every kaftan he has owned since secondary school. “He knows my shoulders better than my wife,” he said, and then asked us not to print that. We are printing it.

body.quote: The cap tells you where someone’s grandmother is from. The sandals tell you how much they earn.

children.text: Footwear was the most competitive category: leather sandals from Kano, polished to a high shine, many with a woven strap across the toe. Caps ranged from the folded fila to tall embroidered hula in every shade from cream to deep wine. The women we photographed were fewer but bolder: long abayas in olive and rust, worn with gold jewellery and printed silk scarves wrapped high and full. One woman paired a black abaya with white trainers and a tiny embroidered handbag, and was the most photographed person of the three weeks.

It is easy to treat Friday dressing as tradition and leave it there. What struck us was how personal it is. Within a shared code, every outfit was a small, considered choice, from the colour of a thread to the angle of a cap, and most of them were excellent. Lagos has louder streets. Abuja, on a Friday afternoon, has better tailoring.

title: Menswear at the shows: the soft tailoring we cannot stop thinking about
excerpt: Unlined jackets, roomy trousers and suits built for 32 degrees. Lagos menswear finally dressed for the weather it lives in.

children.text: For a long time, a suit in Lagos was an act of endurance. Heavy wool, full canvas, shoulder pads built for a London winter, worn from an air-conditioned car to an air-conditioned office with a quick sweat in between. This season’s menswear finally asked a reasonable question: what if a jacket was designed for the city it is worn in?

body.caption: An unlined linen jacket in tobacco brown, worn with pleated trousers and leather slides.
body.alt: An unlined linen jacket in tobacco brown, worn with pleated trousers and leather slides.

children.text: What changed

The answer came in three parts. First, fabric: linen, cotton, light wool blends and, more than once, hand-woven cloth from the north that breathes better than anything imported. Second, construction: jackets with no lining, no padding and soft shoulders that follow the body. Third, proportion: trousers with a full leg and a high waist, cut to let air move. Tunde Bakare, whose label showed on the second night, sent out eighteen looks without a single tie. His jackets closed with one button set low, and several had side vents deep enough to sit down in comfortably. “I made them for my friends who ride okada to meetings,” he said backstage, laughing. “They need to move.”

body.quote: A suit should not be a punishment. My grandfather wore a buba and sokoto to the bank and looked better than any banker.

children.text: The palette was warm and earthy: tobacco, clay, bitter-leaf green, the pale gold of dried guinea corn. Black appeared mostly in the evening looks, and even then in a matte cotton rather than anything with a sheen. Shirts were collarless or worn open, and the shoes were almost all slides, sandals or soft loafers from Aba. Two designers showed jackets with patch pockets big enough for a phone, a wallet and a folded fan, which may be the most Lagos detail of the season.

Prices for this kind of tailoring are not small. A made-to-measure unlined jacket from the labels we liked starts at around ₦180,000, and the waiting time is six weeks. But it lasts, it can be washed, and it can be worn more days of the year than any winter suit. If the shows are a guide, the next time you see a Lagos man in a jacket, he might actually be comfortable.

title: EKPO Editorial: Harmattan Blue
excerpt: Shot at dawn in Kano, a study in indigo and dust with pieces from five northern designers.

children.text: We had four mornings and about forty usable minutes on each. Harmattan light in Kano does something particular just after sunrise: the dust in the air catches the low sun and turns everything into a soft, even haze, like shooting through gauze. By eight it is gone, replaced by a hard white glare. So the crew was up at four, in position by half past five, and packing up before the city was properly awake.

body.caption: Look one: a hand-dyed indigo robe by Rabi Danjuma against the pale walls near the old city gate.
body.alt: Look one: a hand-dyed indigo robe by Rabi Danjuma against the pale walls near the old city gate.

children.text: Why indigo

Kano has been dyeing cloth in indigo for centuries, and the dye pits at Kofar Mata are still working. We wanted the clothes to speak to that history without becoming a costume drama. So the brief to stylist Amina Yusuf was simple: deep blue, layered, and designed by people who live within a day’s drive of the pits. She came back with pieces from five northern labels. There are wide trousers that pool at the ankle, a structured jacket in glazed indigo that shines like wet slate, and a long tunic whose embroidery was done by hand in a single afternoon at the dyers’ compound while we waited.

body.quote: In harmattan, everything is the same colour as the sky. The blue was the only thing that stood up to it.

children.text: We did not use a single light. Every image was made with what the morning gave us, plus two white sheets held by assistants to bounce light into faces. The dust got into everything: lenses, hair, the folds of every garment. We stopped fighting it on day two and started shooting into it. The model, Hadiza, grew up four streets from the dye pits and knew several of the dyers by name, which made for the warmest set we have worked on all year. On the last morning, the dyers asked for prints. They are on their way.

body.caption: Look four: layered indigo shirting, dust rising behind the model in the early wind.
body.alt: Look four: layered indigo shirting, dust rising behind the model in the early wind.

title: EKPO Editorial: Market Day
excerpt: Balogun Market as a set, traders as co-stars, and a wardrobe built entirely from its stalls.

children.text: The rule was that nothing could come from outside. Every garment, shoe and accessory in this story was bought inside Balogun Market on the day of the shoot, with a budget of ₦250,000 and a stylist who knows the lanes better than most traders. Then we turned around and photographed it right there, among the people who sold it to us.

body.caption: A wax-print two-piece bought forty metres from where it was photographed.
body.alt: A wax-print two-piece bought forty metres from where it was photographed.

children.text: Stylist Bisola Martins started at seven in the morning with a list and abandoned it by eight. The best finds were unplanned: a bolt of mustard lace that became a draped skirt, held with safety pins and a leather belt from the next stall; a pair of white trainers bargained down from ₦18,000 to ₦11,500; a stack of plastic bangles in every colour, bought by the dozen. A tailor with a treadle machine under an umbrella took in a pair of trousers in twelve minutes and charged ₦1,500, with a lecture about our model’s posture thrown in for free.

The traders became part of the set without our asking. Mama Gbemi, who sells George fabric near the Nnamdi Azikiwe Street end, adjusted a headwrap on our model without a word and then refused payment. A shoe seller lent us a ladder. A teenage boy carrying pure water sachets walked into one frame and, at his request, stayed in it.

body.quote: Balogun is already the biggest fashion show in Nigeria. We just pointed a camera at it.

children.text: Shoot notes

Balogun is loud, crowded and constantly moving, which makes it hard to shoot and impossible to fake. We worked fast, mostly handheld, in fifteen-minute bursts between deliveries, with one assistant whose only job was to watch for wheelbarrows. By three in the afternoon the light had dropped behind the buildings and the crowd had doubled, and we called it. Everything we bought was donated afterwards to a tailoring school in Mushin, where the mustard lace has, we are told, already become two dresses.

title: EKPO Editorial: Raffia and Chrome
excerpt: Traditional raffia craft meets metallic tailoring in our biggest shoot of the year.

children.text: The idea started with a single object: a raffia hat made by a weaver in Ikot Ekpene, sitting on a desk next to a silver laptop. The contrast was so sharp that we built a whole shoot around it. Raffia, one of the oldest materials in southern Nigeria, set against chrome and metallic fabric, the most synthetic thing we could find.

body.caption: A hand-woven raffia cape over a liquid silver slip dress.
body.alt: A hand-woven raffia cape over a liquid silver slip dress.

children.text: Four weeks of weaving

Ikot Ekpene has been known for its raffia work for generations, and the weavers there still make bags, mats and hats by hand from palm fibre. We commissioned three pieces from a workshop run by Mfon Akpan and her two sisters: a cape, a structured collar and a long fringed skirt. They took four weeks. The skirt alone used fibre from more than sixty palm fronds. Against them, stylist Ekemini Udo paired metallic tailoring from two Lagos labels: a mirrored silver blazer, wide trousers in a pewter lamé, and a slip dress so reflective that it picked up the colour of every wall we stood near.

body.quote: Raffia is soft and alive. Chrome is hard and cold. Put them together and suddenly you can see both properly.

children.text: We shot over two days in a disused printing works in Ikeja, its old steel machinery giving us the industrial backdrop the chrome needed. The raffia had to be misted with water every hour to stop it cracking under the lights. Every image here was lit with a single large source to the side, so the metal flares and the fibre falls into deep shadow. It was our most ambitious production of the year, with a crew of fourteen and a catering bill we will not discuss. The weavers came to Lagos for the second day and saw their work under studio lights for the first time. Mfon took more photographs than our photographer did.

body.caption: Detail: the fringed raffia skirt, made from more than sixty palm fronds.

title: EKPO Editorial: Calabar Carnival
excerpt: Colour, feathers and sequins from the streets of Africa's biggest street party.

children.text: This episode of EKPO TV began last December, when we sent a two-person crew to Calabar with a camera, a sound recorder and very little plan. The carnival closes the year in Cross River, and its parade day fills the city with bands, each one competing in costume, music and choreography. We followed one of them from the workshop to the road, and spent the months since cutting nineteen hours of footage down to eighteen minutes.

body.caption: Final fittings in the band’s workshop, two nights before parade day.
body.alt: Final fittings in the band’s workshop, two nights before parade day.

children.text: Inside the workshop

The band we followed works out of a warehouse near Marian Road. For six weeks before the parade, it is a costume factory: sixty volunteers gluing sequins, cutting foam, stitching feathers onto wire frames. Costume designer Etimbuk Asuquo sketches every piece by hand and keeps the drawings in a box under his table. The film spends most of its running time in that room. You watch a headdress grow from a bare wire circle into something taller than the woman wearing it. You hear the arguments about colour, the music playing on a phone speaker, the moment at three in the morning when everybody stops to eat rice from the same pot.

body.quote: People see the parade and think it is one day. It is two months of our lives, and every sequin is somebody’s evening.

children.text: Parade day is the last six minutes, filmed from inside the band as it moved through the city. We kept the camera at dancer height, which means a lot of feathers in the lens. We would not change it. The sound mix is almost entirely what the street sounded like: drums, whistles, a thousand people singing slightly different words to the same song. The full episode is on EKPO TV now. Watch it with the volume up, and stay for the credits, which roll over the sound of the workshop cleaning up.

title: EKPO Editorial: Night Bus
excerpt: A fashion film following three friends across Lagos after midnight.

children.text: Night Bus is twelve minutes long and has almost no dialogue. Three friends leave a party in Surulere at a quarter past midnight, miss the last ride home they had arranged, and cross the city by danfo, keke and foot until the sun comes up over the Third Mainland Bridge. Everything they wear is by Lagos designers. None of it is explained.

body.caption: A still from the opening scene: three friends under the sodium lights outside a Surulere bus stop.
body.alt: A still from the opening scene: three friends under the sodium lights outside a Surulere bus stop.

children.text: Director Chiamaka Obi wanted to make a fashion film that did not look like an advert. Her rule was that the clothes had to survive the night the way real clothes do. Hems get dusty, a jacket ends up tied around a waist, a borrowed scarf changes hands twice. By the end, the outfits look lived in, which is exactly the point. Stylist Ugo Nnaji pulled from six labels and chose pieces that move: a long pleated skirt that catches the wind from a moving bus, a reflective windbreaker that glows when headlights hit it, and loafers made in Aba that one of the actors walked about four kilometres in during the shoot.

body.quote: Lagos at night is the most cinematic city I know. We did not light it. We just waited for it to light itself.

children.text: Shooting after dark

The film was made over three nights with a crew of seven and one hired danfo, whose driver, Alhaji Sule, became the film’s fourth character. He knew every shortcut, refused to drive faster than the scene required, and improvised the only line of dialogue in the film. Almost every shot uses available light: streetlamps, phone screens, the red glow of a suya grill. The score was composed by a producer from Ajegunle and recorded in a single take, and the final scene was shot in eleven minutes, the time it took the sun to clear the lagoon.

title: EKPO Editorial: Threaded
excerpt: Five sculptural hairstyles built with black thread, the old way, by a braider who learned from her grandmother in Ilesa.

children.text: Threading, or irun kiko, is one of the oldest ways of styling hair in this part of the world. Sections of hair are wrapped tightly in black thread, from root to tip, until they become flexible stems that can be bent into almost any shape. It protects the hair, it lasts for weeks, and in the right hands it becomes sculpture. We wanted to find those hands.

body.caption: Look one: a crown of upward threaded stems, bent at the tips like opening petals.
body.alt: Look one: a crown of upward threaded stems, bent at the tips like opening petals.

children.text: The braider

Yetunde Fakorede learned threading from her grandmother in Ilesa, sitting on the floor between her knees every Saturday from the age of six. She now runs a small salon in Ogba and is, by her own estimate, one of perhaps a dozen people in Lagos who can still do the elaborate pieces. Each look in this story took her between three and six hours. She came to the shoot with three spools of thread, a comb and a plastic bag of hair extensions, and refused any help. The tallest style, a lattice of stems arching over the head and back down to the nape, took five and a half hours and stood about thirty centimetres high.

body.quote: My grandmother said threading is patience you can wear. Every girl in the street could read it.

children.text: We kept everything else out of the way. The models wore plain black jersey, no jewellery and minimal make-up, and we shot against a single grey backdrop with soft overhead light. The point was for the shapes to read clearly, the way a sculpture would in a gallery, and for the thread itself, wound so tightly it shines, to carry the picture. Between looks, the models sat with Yetunde and asked her to teach them the basic wrap. By the end of the day, two of them could do it. Yetunde takes bookings at her salon, with simple styles from ₦7,000. The sculptural pieces are by arrangement. Bring a book.

title: Five exhibitions to see in Lagos this month
excerpt: Paintings, textiles and a room-sized installation made of cassette tape. Our pick of what is on and where.

children.text: October is the busiest month of the Lagos art calendar, and it is easy to spend a weekend driving between openings without really looking at anything. So we narrowed it down. These are the five shows we went back to, and the ones we think deserve a slow hour of your time. Most of the galleries are open Tuesday to Saturday, from 10am to 6pm, but hours shift around events, so check before you set off.

body.caption: Installation view of Side B, with forty thousand metres of unspooled cassette tape.
body.alt: Installation view of Side B, with forty thousand metres of unspooled cassette tape.

children.text: Side B, at Ọ̀rọ̀ House, Ikoyi

Artist Lekan Durojaiye collected more than three thousand old cassettes from markets across the southwest and unspooled every one. The tape hangs from the ceiling in long curtains you walk through, and it rustles as you move, a sound like dry leaves or distant applause. Somewhere in it are sermons, love songs and somebody’s recorded birthday message. Free entry, and best visited on a weekday when the room is quiet.

body.quote: I wanted the tape to sound like a city trying to remember itself.

children.text: Four more worth the drive

Cloth Memory, at the Ebute Gallery, Yaba: twenty textile works by Nkechi Anozie, made from her late mother’s wrappers, cut and restitched into large wall hangings. The colours are faded in a way you cannot fake. Until 1 November.

New Lagos Painters, at Studio Ahiajoku, Victoria Island: a group show of nine painters under thirty. Look for Temi Ogundipe’s small, intense portraits of danfo conductors, each one painted from life at a bus stop.
Above Us, at Kò Kò Gallery, Lekki: photographs of Lagos rooftops, taken from drones and from ladders, by Ifeoluwa Sanni. Water tanks, satellite dishes and laundry lines become pure geometry.

The Weight of Brass, at the Eko Arts Centre, Lagos Island: Chidi Ezenwa’s cast-brass figures, made with foundry workers in Awka. Heavy, quiet and best seen in the late afternoon, when the light comes in from the west windows.

If you only have one afternoon, pair Side B with Cloth Memory. They are a short drive apart, and both are about the same thing in different materials: what ordinary objects hold onto after the people who used them are gone.

title: The photographer documenting Nigeria's disappearing cinemas
excerpt: For six years she has photographed the old picture houses of Kano, Ibadan and Enugu before they close.

children.text: The first cinema Maryam Abdullahi photographed had already stopped showing films. It was 2020, in Kano, and the building had become a warehouse for plastic chairs. The projection booth was still there, though, and so was the screen, grey with dust and torn at one corner. She took one picture of it and spent the next six years looking for others.

body.caption: The auditorium of a closed picture house in Ibadan, photographed in 2023.
body.alt: The auditorium of a closed picture house in Ibadan, photographed in 2023.

children.text: Her project, which she calls Last Show, now includes more than forty buildings in eleven cities. Some are still open in some form, screening football or hosting church services. Many have been converted into shops, offices or event halls. A few have been demolished since she visited, and her photographs are the only detailed record of what they looked like inside. Maryam shoots on a medium-format film camera, mostly in the early morning, and always with permission from whoever owns or guards the building. She often spends a full day in a single place, talking to former projectionists, ticket sellers and neighbours, and recording their memories alongside the pictures.

body.quote: Every old man in the north has a story about the cinema. Where he met his wife, which film he saw ten times, who was thrown out for shouting at the screen.

children.text: What the buildings say

Looking through her archive, patterns appear. Many of the cinemas were built in the 1950s and 1960s, with curved facades, terrazzo floors and names painted in tall letters. Several have hand-painted signs still visible under layers of later paint. The interiors are often surprisingly intact: rows of fold-down seats, ticket booths with brass grilles, posters peeling from the walls. In one Enugu building she found a ledger of ticket sales from 1971, every evening recorded in the same careful blue handwriting.

body.caption: A hand-painted ticket price board, still on the wall of a former cinema in Enugu.
body.alt: A hand-painted ticket price board, still on the wall of a former cinema in Enugu.

children.text: Maryam is now working on a book and hopes to exhibit the full series next year, with the recorded interviews playing in the gallery. She is still looking for buildings, particularly in the east and the Middle Belt. If you know of one, she would like to hear from you before it is gone.

title: Meet the sculptor turning scrap metal into masquerades
excerpt: His life-size works reimagine Ekpo and Egungun costumes in welded steel and car parts.

children.text: Okon Effiong’s studio in Uyo is a yard full of broken cars. Some still have their number plates. Others have been stripped to the frame, their doors, bonnets and exhaust pipes stacked by size along the back wall. In the middle of it all stands a figure nearly three metres tall, its face a grille from an old Peugeot, its body covered in hundreds of overlapping strips of steel cut to look like raffia. It is a masquerade, or rather, it is Okon’s version of one. He grew up watching Ekpo masquerades during festival season in his village in Akwa Ibom, and the memory of those figures, part frightening and part thrilling, runs through everything he makes.

body.caption: Okon Effiong with an unfinished Ekpo figure in his Uyo studio yard.
body.alt: Okon Effiong with an unfinished Ekpo figure in his Uyo studio yard.

children.text: From mechanic to artist

Okon trained as a mechanic before he trained as an artist. He spent eight years repairing cars in a roadside workshop and began welding sculptures from leftover parts in the evenings. His first pieces were small animals: a goat from a gearbox, a cockerel made of spark plugs. The masquerades came later, after a friend showed him photographs of Egungun costumes from the southwest and he noticed how much the layered cloth resembled overlapping metal.

body.quote: A car is like a masquerade. It carries people, it makes noise, and when it dies, its spirit goes somewhere else.

children.text: Each figure takes between two and four months. Okon starts with a rough frame of welded rods, then builds outwards, cutting and shaping each piece by hand with an angle grinder and a pair of heavy shears. He does not paint the metal. Rust is allowed, even encouraged, and some of his older works have turned a deep orange-brown that he considers part of the finished piece. Neighbours bring him parts now, and he keeps a notebook of where each one came from.

body.caption: Detail: strips of cut bonnet steel arranged like raffia fringing.
body.alt: Detail: strips of cut bonnet steel arranged like raffia fringing.

children.text: His work has been shown in group exhibitions in Lagos and Port Harcourt, and he is preparing for his first solo show next year. Moving a three-metre steel masquerade is its own problem, and he is still working out how. For now, the figures stand in the yard among the cars they came from, waiting.

title: Forty years of faces: inside an Onitsha studio's portrait archive
excerpt: A family photo studio near the Main Market kept every negative since 1981. A young archivist is finally printing them.

children.text: Behind the counter of Ezeudu Photos, a small studio a short walk from Onitsha’s Main Market, there is a door that was not opened for almost ten years. Behind it are forty-one cardboard boxes, each one packed with paper envelopes, each envelope holding the negatives from a single day of portraits. The earliest is dated March 1981. The studio was founded by Cyril Ezeudu, who photographed weddings, graduations, newborns and traders for more than three decades. His son still runs the business today, mostly printing passport photos. It was his granddaughter, Amarachi Ezeudu, a history graduate, who decided to see what was in the boxes.

body.caption: A 1984 portrait from the archive: two sisters in matching lace, posed against a painted garden backdrop.
body.alt: A 1984 portrait from the archive: two sisters in matching lace, posed against a painted garden backdrop.

children.text: What she found

So far, Amarachi has scanned about nine thousand negatives, a small fraction of the total. The pictures are a record of how a commercial city dressed, posed and presented itself across four decades. There are traders in their best agbada, schoolchildren in pressed uniforms, couples in matching George wrappers, and a whole series of young men in the late 1980s who all seem to have borrowed the same pair of sunglasses. The painted backdrops change too, from a garden with a fountain to a city skyline to, briefly in 1992, a jet aeroplane.

body.quote: My grandfather never threw anything away. He used to say the customer might come back. Now their grandchildren are coming back.

children.text: The most moving part of the project has been finding the subjects. Amarachi posts selected images online and asks people to identify themselves or their relatives. More than two hundred families have come forward. Some have never seen these pictures; for others, it is the only photograph they have of a parent. She prints each family a copy for free and asks only that they tell her the story behind it.

body.caption: Amarachi Ezeudu sorting negatives in the studio’s back room.
body.alt: Amarachi Ezeudu sorting negatives in the studio’s back room.

children.text: A first selection of eighty prints goes on show in Enugu early next year. Amarachi hopes eventually to scan the entire archive and keep it in Onitsha, where it was made. The boxes, she says, are staying in the back room. The door is open now.

title: The painter who works only in blue biro
excerpt: Enugu artist Obiageli Nnaji makes vast, detailed portraits with the cheapest pen in the country. Each one takes about three hundred pens.

children.text: There is a cardboard box in the corner of Obiageli Nnaji’s studio in Enugu, and it is full of empty pens. Plain blue ballpoints, the same kind every Nigerian schoolchild has chewed on during an exam. She keeps them all. By her count, the box holds a little over four thousand, and each one represents a few hours of drawing.

body.caption: A detail from Mama Ngozi, built up from thousands of fine crosshatched lines.
body.alt: A detail from Mama Ngozi, built up from thousands of fine crosshatched lines.

children.text: Why biro

Obiageli studied fine art at university and trained as a painter, but she could not afford oil paints after graduating. A box of fifty biros cost her ₦1,500. She started drawing her neighbours with them, and found she liked the restriction. Blue ink, she says, forces her to think about light in a completely different way, because there is no white to add back in. Every highlight has to be planned from the first stroke and protected for months. Her portraits are large, often more than two metres tall, and made on heavy paper joined in panels. Up close, the faces dissolve into thousands of tiny crosshatched strokes; from across the room, they look almost photographic.

body.quote: Everybody in Nigeria has held this pen. When they see what it can do, they remember their own hand.

children.text: Her subjects are mostly people she knows: the woman who sells roasted corn at the end of her street, a retired schoolteacher, her younger brother on his wedding day. She asks each sitter to choose how they want to be shown, and spends several afternoons with them before she begins, mostly talking and drinking tea rather than drawing. A single large portrait takes about four months and around three hundred pens. She works six days a week, usually from early morning until the light goes, and listens to old highlife records while she draws.

body.caption: Obiageli Nnaji at work in her Enugu studio, with the box of finished pens beside her.
body.alt: Obiageli Nnaji at work in her Enugu studio, with the box of finished pens beside her.

children.text: Visitors to the studio almost always ask the same question: what happens if she makes a mistake? Her answer is that she does not erase, she absorbs. A wrong line becomes a shadow, a crease, a strand of hair. Her first solo exhibition is planned for Lagos in the new year. Until then, she is drawing, and the box keeps filling up.

title: Review: a Port Harcourt show about the rivers that made the city
excerpt: Twelve artists, one warehouse by the waterfront, and an exhibition that smells faintly of mangrove mud. It is the best show we have seen this year.

children.text: The first thing you notice is the sound. As you walk into Tide Line, the new show at the Creek Road Art House in Port Harcourt, a low recording plays from speakers hidden in the rafters: water against wooden hulls, an outboard motor, women calling to each other across a creek. It runs for forty minutes and then loops. Most visitors stay for all of it. The exhibition brings together twelve artists from across the Niger Delta, all responding to the rivers and creeks that shaped Port Harcourt and the communities around it. The curator, Ibiere Dagogo, grew up in Bonny and spent two years visiting artists by boat to put it together.

body.caption: Installation view of Tide Line, with Boma Jack’s suspended canoe in the foreground.
body.alt: Installation view of Tide Line, with Boma Jack’s suspended canoe in the foreground.

children.text: The highlights

The centrepiece is a full-size wooden canoe by Boma Jack, hung from the ceiling and carved along its inside with hundreds of small figures: fishermen, traders, children, a wedding party. You have to crouch and look up to see them, which feels deliberate. Elsewhere, Tamara Ebi’s photographs of fishing families in Kalabari communities are large, quiet and very beautiful, printed on a matte paper that makes the water look like slate. Nengi Brown’s textile works, made from old fishing nets dyed in mangrove bark, hang in long curtains along the back wall. The room genuinely smells faintly of the creek.

body.quote: People talk about the Delta as if it were only a problem. I wanted a room where it is a home first.

children.text: The verdict

Not every work lands. A video piece near the entrance feels unfinished, and the wall texts could be half as long. But as a whole, Tide Line is generous, moving and carefully made. It treats its subject with love rather than despair, and it reminds you that some of the most exciting work in the country is happening outside Lagos, in rooms that most critics have not yet visited.

Tide Line runs until 30 November. Entry is ₦2,000, free for students on Thursdays. Go in the late afternoon, when the light through the warehouse windows turns the nets gold, and give the soundtrack the full forty minutes.

title: The new guard of Nigerian design
excerpt: Six designers under thirty on building brands in Lagos, making clothes for Nigerians first, and why the world is paying attention.

children.text: We brought them together on a Sunday afternoon in a borrowed studio in Ikoyi: six designers, all under thirty, all running their own labels from Lagos. Between them they employ more than ninety people, sell in eleven countries and make almost everything within a few hours’ drive of where they sleep. None of them had met all the others before. By the end of the afternoon, they were sharing tailors’ phone numbers.

body.caption: The cover: left to right, Tolu Bankole, Ada Ike, Seyi Lawson, Kasim Danladi, Ebi Tonye and Funmi Akande.
body.alt: The cover: left to right, Tolu Bankole, Ada Ike, Seyi Lawson, Kasim Danladi, Ebi Tonye and Funmi Akande.

children.text: Nigerians first

The thing they agreed on fastest was who they design for. Ada Ike, 27, whose label makes structured dresses in Akwete cloth, put it simply: “My first customer is my cousin in Enugu. If she will not wear it to a wedding, it does not leave the studio.” Kasim Danladi, 29, who makes menswear in hand-woven northern cloth, said almost the same about his uncles in Kaduna. Production was the topic that took longest. All six make in Nigeria, and all six described the same challenges: diesel costs, the price of imported trims, and finding skilled machinists. Funmi Akande, 28, now runs a small training programme in her Surulere workshop, paying apprentices while they learn. Ebi Tonye, 25, sources almost all her fabric from deadstock dealers in Ikeja and Aba.

body.quote: For a long time, the dream was to be stocked in London. Now London calls us, and we tell them to wait for the next production run.
body.cite: Seyi Lawson, 26, founder of Lawson Studio

children.text: Tolu Bankole, 29, the oldest of the group, has been doing this the longest. He started selling shirts from the boot of his car seven years ago. “Nobody gave us permission,” he said. “We just kept making things until people noticed.” Asked why the world is paying attention now, they had different answers: social media, a global appetite for clothes with a story, a generation of Nigerians abroad who want to wear home. But they kept coming back to one idea. The work is simply good now, made with care and confidence, and it no longer asks anyone for approval.

body.caption: Behind the scenes: Ada Ike adjusts a sleeve on Kasim Danladi’s jacket between shots.
body.alt: Behind the scenes: Ada Ike adjusts a sleeve on Kasim Danladi’s jacket between shots.

children.text: The afternoon ended with jollof from a nearby buka and a long argument about whether a buba can ever be cropped. It was not resolved. We suspect it will be, on a runway, soon.

title: "I stopped designing for Europe and started designing for my aunties"
excerpt: The founder of one of Lagos' fastest-growing labels on building a brand that looks like home.

children.text: Bimpe Alade spent the first three years of her label trying to look like somewhere else. Her early collections were minimalist, neutral and, by her own admission, a little cold. They sold modestly, mostly online, mostly to customers abroad. Then, at a family wedding in Abeokuta in 2022, she watched her aunties walk in, and everything changed. Her label, Àlàdé, now sells out most of its drops within days. We met at her studio in Ebute Metta, where the rails are full of marigold, coral and a green she calls okra.

body.caption: Bimpe Alade in her Ebute Metta studio, surrounded by rails of the new collection.
body.alt: Bimpe Alade in her Ebute Metta studio, surrounded by rails of the new collection.

children.text: What happened at that wedding? “My aunties came in wearing aso-ebi in this incredible gold, with the gele so high, and they were the most confident women in the room. I was standing there in a beige dress I had designed, and I felt invisible. I went home and looked at my whole collection and thought, who is this for? Not for them. Not for me either.” How did the clothes change? “Colour first. Then volume. I started looking at how Nigerian women actually move in clothes: they dance, they kneel to greet elders, they carry babies on their backs. Everything has to allow for that. My trousers have more room in the hip now. My dresses have pockets deep enough for a phone and a fan.”

body.quote: My aunties are my fit models now. If my Aunty Kemi says the armhole is tight, it is tight.

children.text: The business of home

And the business? “It grew because people here could see themselves in it. Lagos customers became the biggest group almost overnight. Then something funny happened: the customers abroad came back too, because now the clothes had a point of view. You cannot design for everybody. You design for somebody, properly, and everybody else finds you.”

What comes next? “A bigger workshop, hopefully next year. Right now we are twelve people, and I want to train more young women as machinists. And I am making a collection for older women, sixty and above. Nobody designs for them, and they have the most money and the best parties. That is a mistake.”

body.caption: A look from Àlàdé’s current collection: wide trousers and a gathered top in marigold cotton.
body.alt: A look from Àlàdé’s current collection: wide trousers and a gathered top in marigold cotton.

title: In conversation: the stylist behind this year's biggest music videos
excerpt: How a self-taught stylist from Aba ended up dressing half the Afrobeats charts.

children.text: Chukwudi Okeke, known to almost everyone as Chuks, does not have a fashion degree. He has a diploma in accounting, a phone with eleven thousand contacts and a storage unit in Ikeja packed so full of clothes that he has to step sideways to get in. Over the past two years, he has styled more than forty music videos. We talked over pepper soup in Ikeja, between fittings.

body.caption: Chuks in his Ikeja storage unit, which he calls the archive.
body.alt: Chuks in his Ikeja storage unit, which he calls the archive.

children.text: Aba, okrika and a ₦50,000 budget

How did you start? “In Aba, my uncle had a shop selling second-hand clothes. Every Saturday I would sort the bales with him, and I learned to see quality fast: the stitching, the fabric, what a piece is worth. When I moved to Lagos, a friend was making a music video with no budget, and I said I could dress everybody for ₦50,000. I did it from okrika. That video went everywhere.” What makes a good music video look? “It has to work at three seconds and at three minutes. People scroll, so the first frame must stop them. But it also has to hold up when they watch it again and again. I always ask the artist: who are you in this song? Not who are you in general. In this song.”

body.quote: A music video is not a runway. Nobody walks in a straight line. They dance, they sweat, they fall on the floor. The clothes must survive.

children.text: Where do the clothes come from now? “Half from young Nigerian designers, half from markets. I love putting a ₦3,000 shirt from Yaba next to a piece that costs ₦300,000. The camera does not know the price. I also make a lot of things myself now. My tailor in Aba makes custom pieces for me in three days, and he sends them by bus with a note in the pocket.”

What would you tell someone starting out? “Learn to sew a button. Learn to steam. Learn to carry safety pins in every pocket. And say yes to the small jobs, because the people on small jobs become the people on big jobs. Everybody I work with now, I met when none of us had money.”

body.caption: Rails ready for a two-day video shoot, each hanger tagged with a scene number.
body.alt: Rails ready for a two-day video shoot, each hanger tagged with a scene number.

title: Five questions with a Calabar chef
excerpt: On pepper soup, family recipes and opening a restaurant in her grandmother's house.

children.text: Arit Okon opened her restaurant, Ufọk Eka, in the house where her grandmother raised eleven children. It has eight tables, a menu that changes with the market, and a pepper soup that people in Calabar argue about. We asked her five questions on a quiet Tuesday afternoon, while a pot of afang simmered behind her and a radio played highlife in the next room.

body.caption: Arit Okon in the kitchen of Ufọk Eka, in her grandmother’s former house in Calabar.
body.alt: Arit Okon in the kitchen of Ufọk Eka, in her grandmother’s former house in Calabar.

children.text: One: why open in your grandmother’s house? “Because it was empty, and because it was the kitchen I learned in. My grandmother cooked for twenty people every day in this house. When she passed, nobody wanted to sell it, but nobody wanted to live in it either. So I filled it with people again.” Two: what makes Calabar food different? “Patience and vegetables. Efik cooking uses a lot of leaves, like afang, waterleaf and ukazi, and they have to be cut very fine, by hand. You cannot rush it. And we are generous with seafood, because the water is close.”
The pepper soup question

Three: tell us about the pepper soup. “It is my grandmother’s recipe, with one change she would not approve of: I add a little smoked fish to the stock at the beginning. The spices I grind myself every morning. People ask me for the recipe and I give it to them, and they still come back, so it must be the hands.”

body.quote: A recipe is only the map. The road is your hands.
body.cite: Arit Okon, chef and owner of Ufọk Eka

children.text: Four: what is the hardest part of running the restaurant? “The market. Prices change every week. Some weeks periwinkle is cheap and I put it in everything; some weeks it is gold. I change the menu each morning based on what I can buy, and I write it on a board by the door.” Five: where do you eat on your day off? “At my mother’s house. I do not cook, and she does not let me into her kitchen. It is the best meal of the week, and I am not allowed to say anything about the salt.”
Ufọk Eka is open Tuesday to Sunday for lunch and dinner, with mains from ₦6,500. There are no reservations for lunch, so arrive before one or be ready to wait on the veranda with a cold zobo.

title: The DJ who plays only Nigerian vinyl
excerpt: Thousands of records, all pressed between 1965 and 1985, and a Friday night that sells out every week.

children.text: Every Friday night at a small bar in Surulere, a DJ who calls himself Baba Wax plays records for five hours without repeating a song. Every one of them was pressed in Nigeria between 1965 and 1985. The bar holds about a hundred and twenty people, and every week there is a line outside by ten. His real name is Olumide Akinyemi, he is thirty-four, and he talked to us on a Thursday afternoon while cleaning records with a soft brush.

body.caption: Olumide Akinyemi, aka Baba Wax, behind the decks on a Friday night in Surulere.
body.alt: Olumide Akinyemi, aka Baba Wax, behind the decks on a Friday night in Surulere.

children.text: Where did the collection come from? “It started with my father’s records, maybe two hundred. When he passed, I could not let them go. Then I started buying from market traders in Ibadan, from old men clearing out their houses, from radio stations throwing out their libraries. Now I have about six thousand. My wife says that is enough. I disagree.” Why only that period? “Those twenty years were special. Highlife, juju, Afrobeat, Afro-funk, disco from Lagos and Aba, gospel, all of it pressed here, in Nigerian factories, with Nigerian sleeves. The sound quality of some of those pressings is better than anything you hear today. And so much of it has never been reissued. If I do not play it, nobody will hear it.”

body.quote: Young people come for the vibe, and then they ask me who the band is. That question is the whole point.

children.text: The one that got away

Who comes on Friday nights? “Everybody. University students, aunties, uncles who remember the songs from the first time, tourists, designers. Sometimes I see three generations of one family on the floor together. Nobody is on their phone for long, because the records do not stop.” And the hardest record to find? “The ones that were only pressed once, in small numbers, for a local band that played weddings in one town. I have been looking for one particular highlife single from Owerri for nine years. I know it exists. An old man sang it to me once.”

body.caption: A small section of the six-thousand-record collection, filed by year and city.
body.alt: A small section of the six-thousand-record collection, filed by year and city.

children.text: Baba Wax plays every Friday from 10pm. Entry is ₦5,000. If you have a box of old records in your father’s house, he would very much like to talk to you.

title: Five questions with a Kano leatherworker
excerpt: Bilkisu Sani makes bags by hand in a workshop her family has run for three generations. She has never advertised, and there is a two-month waiting list.

children.text: Bilkisu Sani’s workshop is a single room off a courtyard in Kano’s old city. Her grandfather tanned and worked goatskin here, and so did her father. She is the first woman in the family to run it. Her bags, satchels and sandals are made entirely by hand, from leather tanned a few streets away, and they are almost impossible to buy without waiting. We asked her five questions.

body.caption: Bilkisu Sani in her workshop, stitching the strap of a saddle bag by hand.
body.alt: Bilkisu Sani in her workshop, stitching the strap of a saddle bag by hand.

children.text: One: how did you learn? “By watching. I was not supposed to be in the workshop, but I sat in the doorway every afternoon after school. My father pretended not to see me. When I was fifteen, he gave me a piece of leather and a needle and said, show me. I have not stopped since.” Two: what makes Kano leather special? “The tanning. It is done slowly, with plant materials, the way it has been done here for hundreds of years. The leather is soft but strong, and it gets better with age. Also the dyes: a deep red, a yellow, a green, which we have always used.”

body.quote: A good bag should outlive the person who bought it. Then it goes to their daughter.

children.text: On waiting, and on training

Three: why is there a waiting list? “Because there is only me and two apprentices. A large bag takes four or five days. I will not make faster, and I will not hire people I have not trained myself. People are welcome to wait.” Four: who buys from you? “Mostly people from Kano, Abuja and Lagos, through word of mouth. Some people buy one bag and then come back years later for their children. A few designers have asked me to make for them. I said yes to one, because she came to the workshop herself and sat in the doorway, like me.”

Five: what would you change about the industry? “I would like young people to see this as a real job. It pays, it is beautiful, and it does not need a factory. I am training two girls now. In five years, I hope they have their own workshops, and I hope they take apprentices who sit in their doorways.”
Bilkisu’s bags start at ₦85,000 for a small pouch and rise with size and detail. Orders are taken by visit or by phone. Bring patience, and if you visit, accept the tea.

title: New music Friday: twelve songs for your weekend
excerpt: Fresh releases from Lagos, Accra and London, handpicked by our music desk.

children.text: It has been a strong week. Two long-awaited singles finally arrived, an Accra producer we have been watching made a quiet masterpiece, and a highlife band from Enugu released a song so joyful we played it four times in the office before lunch. Here are the twelve tracks our music desk could not stop talking about, in roughly the order we would play them on a Friday evening, from the first drink to the last bus home.

body.caption: Enugu highlife band The Nine Mile Orchestra, whose new single opens this week’s list.
body.alt: Enugu highlife band The Nine Mile Orchestra, whose new single opens this week’s list.

children.text: The Nine Mile Orchestra, Okpara Avenue: horns, a talking guitar and a chorus the whole band sings.
Dami Rae, Slow Wine: a late-night love song with a bassline you feel in your chest.
Kofi Mensa-Lartey, Labadi 5am: an Accra producer’s gentle, drifting instrumental.
Ruth Ojo, Mama’s Kitchen: soft alté soul about cooking with her mother.
Big Tunji, No Wahala Pass: pure dancefloor amapiano, built for December.
Aisha Garba, Sahel: Hausa vocals over a minimal electronic beat.
Lolu and the Grandsons, Ferry: Lagos funk with a lot of cowbell.
Zara Nkem, London Rain: a South London singer remembering Enugu.
Ebi Wari, Creek Song: a guitar ballad from Port Harcourt.
Tobe, Danfo Diaries: witty, fast rap about the daily commute.
Ama Darko, Kente Blue: Ghanaian highlife with a modern drum kit.
Ikenna Obi, Last Bus: a stripped piano song to end the night.
Our pick of the week

If you listen to only one, make it Okpara Avenue. The Nine Mile Orchestra are twelve musicians who have played weddings and hotel bars in Enugu for a decade, and this is their first proper studio recording. It sounds like a party you have been trying to get into for years. The guitar solo at the two-minute mark is the best thing we have heard all month, and the backing vocals, slightly out of time and all the better for it, sound like friends rather than session singers.

body.quote: We recorded it live, all twelve of us in one room. If someone made a mistake, we kept it.
body.cite: Chibuzor Eze, bandleader, The Nine Mile Orchestra

children.text: Honourable mention goes to Aisha Garba’s Sahel, which is the strangest and most beautiful thing on the list: four minutes of Hausa vocals, a single synthesiser and long stretches of near silence. It will not be on the radio. It should be. The full playlist is on our profile. Tell us what we missed.

title: Review: a debut album that sounds like Surulere in 1979
excerpt: Live horns, highlife guitars and a very modern voice. Our verdict.

children.text: The first sound on Adunni Fashola’s debut album, Ojúde, is a needle dropping onto a record. It is a slightly obvious gesture, but it sets out her intentions clearly. Over the next forty-two minutes, she builds something that feels lifted from a Surulere nightclub in the late 1970s, then runs it through a very contemporary sensibility.

body.caption: The cover of Ojúde: Adunni Fashola photographed in a vintage studio portrait style.
body.alt: The cover of Ojúde: Adunni Fashola photographed in a vintage studio portrait style.

children.text: The sound

This is a band record. Every track features live musicians, including a five-piece horn section, two guitarists playing interlocking highlife lines, and a drummer who clearly grew up listening to old Afrobeat records. Producer Wale Coker recorded most of it to tape, and you can hear the warmth: the slight hiss, the way the bass blooms. Against that, Adunni’s voice is completely of now. She sings in a mix of Yoruba, English and pidgin, often in the same line, with a cool, unhurried delivery that never tries to imitate the past. The tension between the old arrangement and the new voice is what makes the album work.

body.quote: I wanted my grandmother and my little sister to both like it. That was the only brief.

children.text: Ọjà Oba, the second track, is the obvious single: a bright, galloping song about meeting someone at the market, with a horn hook you will be humming for days. Ìyá Wa slows everything down for a seven-minute tribute to her mother, built over a single repeating guitar figure that never resolves, so the song feels like a held breath. And Third Mainland closes the record with a long, joyful jam that fades out just as it gets wild, which is either a tease or a promise of what the live show will be.
The verdict

The album sags slightly in the middle, where two mid-tempo songs blur together, and the needle-drop gimmick appears once too often. But these are small complaints. Ojúde is a confident, warm and beautifully played debut from an artist who knows exactly what she wants to sound like, and who has surrounded herself with musicians good enough to get her there. Put it on at a party and watch the uncles get up first. Rating: 4 out of 5.

title: The rise of alté: how a scene became a sound
excerpt: Ten years on, the artists who started it look back on where it began.

children.text: A decade ago, alté was less a genre than a group of friends. A few dozen young Lagosians who made music in bedrooms, dressed in thrifted clothes and second-hand sunglasses, and did not care much whether radio played them. The word itself, taken from “alternative”, was used half as a joke. Ten years on, the sound they made can be heard everywhere, from adverts to film scores. We asked some of the people who were there how it happened.

body.caption: An early alté show in a Lekki apartment, around 2016, from the personal archive of a musician who played it.
body.alt: An early alté show in a Lekki apartment, around 2016, from the personal archive of a musician who played it.

children.text: Producer Kayode Banjo, who made beats in his parents’ house in Gbagada, remembers the early shows as tiny and chaotic. “Forty people in somebody’s living room. One speaker. We played each other our songs and argued about them until morning. Nobody was trying to be famous. We were trying to be different.” Singer Tiwa Ogun, who released her first songs online at nineteen, says the scene was defined as much by attitude as by sound. “We were mixing everything: R&B, punk, highlife, dancehall, whatever we liked. Our parents did not understand it. The industry did not understand it. That was the best part.”

body.quote: Alté was never a sound. It was permission to sound like yourself.

children.text: Becoming a sound

Over time, the scene developed recognisable features: slow tempos, soft vocals, hazy production, a love of space and silence. Fashion was part of it too, with a style that mixed vintage Nigerian pieces and streetwear long before it was common. Some artists moved into the mainstream. Others stayed deliberately small, releasing music only to the few thousand people who were already listening. Both paths, everyone we spoke to agreed, were legitimate.

Most of them are wary of nostalgia. Kayode now produces for younger artists who were children when the first shows happened, and says he learns more from them than they do from him. “They hear what we did as history,” he said, laughing. “That is fine. Now it is their job to be weird.”

body.caption: Kayode Banjo in his Gbagada studio, where he still makes most of his music.
body.alt: Kayode Banjo in his Gbagada studio, where he still makes most of his music.

title: Live: our night at a Freedom Park jam session
excerpt: A packed Freedom Park, three surprise guests and a set that ran past 2am.

children.text: By nine o’clock the courtyard at Freedom Park on Lagos Island was full. By ten, people were watching from the steps, the balconies and, in one case, the top of a parked generator. The headliners, a ten-piece Afrobeat collective called Orisun, had not yet played a note, and the crowd was already singing along to the warm-up DJ.

body.caption: Orisun on stage at Freedom Park, with the crowd reaching back to the courtyard walls.
body.alt: Orisun on stage at Freedom Park, with the crowd reaching back to the courtyard walls.

children.text: The set

Orisun came on at half past ten and played for over three hours. Their set was built around long, patient grooves: the rhythm section locking in for minutes at a time before the horns arrived, all at once, like a door blowing open. Bandleader Femi Akintola played saxophone and sang, and conducted the band with small hand signals that the crowd started to copy. The surprises came after midnight. First, a young highlife guitarist from Ibadan, Seun Ajala, joined for two songs and very nearly stole the show. Then a gospel choir of eight walked through the crowd, singing, and climbed onto the stage. Finally, an older trumpeter who played with the band’s founders in the 1990s came out to a roar of recognition from anyone over forty.

body.quote: We never plan the end. We play until the people tell us to stop, and tonight they did not.

children.text: The crowd

What made the night special was the mix. Students in vintage shirts danced next to couples who had clearly been coming to nights like this for decades. A group of aunties in matching ankara held the front row all night and corrected the lyrics of anyone near them. Vendors selling small chops, puff-puff and cold drinks did steady business, and the queue for the bathrooms was, as always, a disgrace.

The band finally stopped at twenty past two, after a last song that lasted almost twenty minutes. Even then, half the crowd stayed, still singing the chorus into the night while the crew coiled cables around them. Tickets for the next session, in November, are ₦10,000. Buy them early, bring cash for the vendors, and do not park anywhere you will need to leave before three.

title: Review: a Calabar singer's quiet, brilliant second record
excerpt: Eno Ekpenyong trades the big production of her debut for guitar, voice and the sound of rain. It is the best Nigerian album of the autumn.

children.text: Eno Ekpenyong’s first album was loud. Big drums, stacked vocals, a hit single built for clubs. It did well, and nobody would have blamed her for making it again. Instead, she went home to Calabar, rented a room above a tailor’s shop on Atekong Road, and recorded her second album, Mbubịt, almost entirely alone with an acoustic guitar.

body.caption: Eno Ekpenyong in the room above the tailor’s shop where she recorded Mbubịt.
body.alt: Eno Ekpenyong in the room above the tailor’s shop where she recorded Mbubịt.

children.text: The record runs to nine songs and thirty-four minutes. Most feature just her voice and guitar, with occasional additions: a cello on two tracks, a field recording of rain on a tin roof, and on one song, the sound of the tailor’s sewing machine downstairs, which she decided to keep. It sounds intimate in a way that very few Nigerian records allow themselves to be. Eno sings mostly in Efik and English, and her voice, which was often buried in effects on the first album, is now right at the front. It is a lovely instrument: low, slightly husky, with a way of holding back on the high notes that makes them land harder when they come.

body.quote: After the first album, I could not hear myself any more. I needed a small room and a lot of quiet to find my voice again.

children.text: The songs

The opening track, Eka, is a letter to her mother, sung so softly you lean towards the speaker. Atekong is a portrait of the street outside her window, full of small details: the pure water seller, the church choir rehearsing on Thursday nights, the boy who fixes phones and sings along to the radio while he works. And the closing song, Edim, which means rain, is simply beautiful, the field recording slowly rising until it drowns the guitar and then, for the last thirty seconds, everything else.

Some listeners who loved the first album will find this one too slow, and there is a stretch near the middle where two guitar figures sound very alike. That is a small price. Mbubịt is brave, personal and beautifully made, a record for late evenings and long drives. It will not fill a dancefloor. It will stay with you much longer. Rating: 4.5 out of 5.

title: Live: highlife till sunrise at a Port Harcourt hotel bar
excerpt: Every Saturday, a band of men in their sixties plays the old songs in a garden bar off Aba Road. We stayed until the last bottle.

children.text: The sign outside the Rosebud Hotel on a side street off Aba Road still says air-conditioned rooms, though the air conditioning is a matter of some debate. Nobody comes for the rooms. They come for the garden bar at the back, where every Saturday night since 1998, a highlife band called the Rosebud Gentlemen has played from about nine until the sun comes up.

body.caption: The Rosebud Gentlemen under the garden lights, with the dancefloor already full at 10pm.
body.alt: The Rosebud Gentlemen under the garden lights, with the dancefloor already full at 10pm.

children.text: The band

There are seven of them, aged between fifty-eight and seventy-one. Guitarist and bandleader Sunday Ibekwe is the youngest member and has led the band for twenty years. Their repertoire is old-school highlife, songs from the 1960s and 1970s, plus a handful of their own compositions, all played without a set list. Sunday calls the next song by playing its first two notes; the others follow. They play in their good clothes: pressed trousers, patterned shirts, polished shoes. The drummer, Pa Christopher, wears a felt hat that he says he has never taken off on stage.

body.quote: We are old, but the songs are older. As long as people dance, we will play.
body.cite: Sunday Ibekwe, bandleader, the Rosebud Gentlemen

children.text: The audience is a mix of regulars who have been coming for decades and younger people who heard about it from a friend. Couples dance the old way, close and slow, with small shuffling steps, and the regulars are happy to teach anyone who asks. Plastic tables fill up with bottles of beer and plates of peppered snail and fresh fish from the grill in the corner, where a woman called Mama Tonye has been cooking on Saturday nights for as long as the band has been playing.

Around two in the morning, the music changes. The band slows down, the lights dim, and the dancefloor fills with couples swaying almost in place. By four, only the most committed remain. When the band finally plays its last song, just after half past five, the sky above the garden is turning grey, and someone always asks for one more. They usually get it.
If you go: entry is free, but buy a drink and tip the band. Tables fill by ten, so arrive early. Dress well, because everyone else will.

title: Orire Studio is weaving the future of aso-oke
excerpt: The Ibadan label works with forty weavers to turn a ceremonial cloth into everyday clothing. We spent a week in their workshop and followed a single jacket from loom to rail.

children.text: The workshop sits on the second floor of a converted printing press in Oke-Ado, Ibadan, and you hear it before you see it: twelve narrow looms working at once, a sound somewhere between rain on a zinc roof and a slow drum. Downstairs, a generator hums. Upstairs, nobody looks up from the warp.

body.caption: Weavers at work in the Orire Studio workshop in Oke-Ado, Ibadan.
body.alt: Weavers at work in the Orire Studio workshop in Oke-Ado, Ibadan.

children.text: Orire Studio was started in 2019 by Morenike Adebanjo, a former bank analyst whose grandmother wove aso-oke in Iseyin. The label now works with forty weavers, twelve in the Ibadan workshop and the rest in their own homes across Oyo State, paid per strip at a rate the studio publishes on its website. What they make is not the stiff, metallic cloth most of us associate with weddings and chieftaincy titles. It is softer, lighter and cut into chore jackets, wide trousers and shirts you could wear to a Tuesday meeting. The trick, Adebanjo explains, is the yarn. Traditional aso-oke uses a dense, shiny thread that holds its shape like card. Orire blends local cotton with a finer spun yarn, sets the looms to a looser tension and washes every strip twice before it is cut. The result drapes. It creases where your elbows bend. It looks better after a year than on the day you buy it.

body.quote: My grandmother made cloth for the three biggest days of a person's life. I wanted to make cloth for the other three hundred and sixty-two.

children.text: One jacket, loom to rail

We followed a single indigo-and-rust chore jacket through the building over five days. It took nineteen strips, each about ten centimetres wide, woven by two people over three days. A pattern cutter named Kunle laid the strips edge to edge and matched the stripes by eye before a tailor joined them with a flat-felled seam so the inside is as clean as the outside. Horn buttons come from a carver in Oyo town. The last step is a stamp on the inside pocket: the weaver's initials and the date the cloth came off the loom.
Weaving: 3 days, 2 weavers, 19 strips
Washing and drying: 1 day
Cutting and matching: half a day
Sewing and finishing: 1 day
Retail price: ₦185,000

That price is not small, and Adebanjo does not pretend otherwise. But the jackets sell out in every drop, and the waiting list for the next run, due in November, is already longer than the run itself. You can find a small edit of Orire pieces in the EKPO shop, and the full collection at the studio's showroom in Bodija, open Thursday to Saturday.

title: The shoe brand making loafers out of Aba leather
excerpt: Hand-stitched, locally tanned and sold out every drop.

children.text: Ariaria Market in Aba has been making shoes for most of West Africa for decades, usually without a name on the insole. Chidubem Okafor wanted to put one there. His label, Nkem Footwear, makes a single style of penny loafer in four colours, and every pair is tanned, cut and stitched within ten kilometres of the market.

body.caption: Nkem Footwear's oxblood loafer on the last at the Aba workshop.
body.alt: Nkem Footwear's oxblood loafer on the last at the Aba workshop.

children.text: Why only one shoe

Okafor started with a range of eight styles in 2022 and lost money on six of them. In 2024 he cut back to the loafer, the shoe his customers kept reordering, and put everything into making it better. The leather now comes from a small tannery in Osisioma that uses vegetable tannins from mangrove bark, which takes six weeks rather than two days but gives a hide that darkens and softens with wear rather than cracking.

The construction is a hand-stitched moccasin: the upper wraps under the foot and is sewn to a separate top piece by one craftsman, Mr Uche, who has been doing it for thirty-one years and can finish four pairs a day. The sole is stitched, not glued, so it can be replaced. Okafor offers resoling for ₦12,000, and says about one customer in five has already used it.

body.quote: People think Aba means cheap. Aba means fast and skilled. I am just asking the skill to slow down.

children.text: Buying a pair

Drops happen on the first Friday of the month, online only, at 10am. A pair costs ₦78,000 and the colours are black, oxblood, a mid-brown called kola, and a suede in tobacco. Sizes run from 39 to 46; Okafor recommends going half a size down if you plan to wear them without socks, which, in Lagos traffic heat, most people do. Each drop is between 120 and 150 pairs, and the last three sold out in under an hour. If you miss one, the brand keeps a short list for returns and cancellations, and it is worth getting on it. Break them in at home for a week before wearing them out. The leather is stiff at first and gives completely by the second month, after which they are, as one EKPO staffer put it, the shoes you forget you have on.

title: A jewellery collaboration with Bida brass casters
excerpt: Old techniques, new shapes, and a collection that sold out in a day.

children.text: Bida, in Niger State, has been known for its brass and glass for centuries. The casters there still use lost-wax casting: a shape is modelled in wax, coated in clay, then heated so the wax runs out and molten brass can be poured into the hollow it leaves behind. Every mould is used once and broken. Lagos jewellery label Salma Ade, run by designer Salma Adeoye, spent eight months working with a family workshop of three brothers in the Masagá quarter of the town on a twenty-piece collection called Ruwa, the Hausa word for water. It went on sale on a Thursday morning in July and was gone by Friday.

body.caption: Wax models for the Ruwa collection, before they are coated in clay.
body.alt: Wax models for the Ruwa collection, before they are coated in clay.

children.text: Who did what

Adeoye drew the shapes: wide cuffs with a rippled surface, long drop earrings like falling water, and a heavy collar made of linked oval plates. The brothers translated the drawings into wax, adjusting thicknesses so the brass would flow evenly, and suggested the hammered texture that ended up on almost every piece. Pricing was agreed before the first piece was cast, and the workshop receives a share of every sale on top of its fee.

body.quote: They corrected my drawings more than I corrected their casting. Half the good ideas in this collection are theirs, and the credit tag says so.
