children.text: That credit tag is a small cotton card in every box naming the workshop and the brother who cast that particular piece. It is a simple gesture, and more labels should copy it. It also means a customer in Abuja or London knows exactly whose hands made the cuff on her wrist, and the brothers say private orders for their own work have doubled since the launch.
Ripple cuff: ₦65,000
Water drop earrings: ₦38,000
Oval plate collar: ₦140,000
Small stacking rings: ₦18,000 each

Brass darkens with time. Adeoye ships every piece with a square of polishing cloth and recommends a paste of lime juice and salt for heavier tarnish, rinsed off quickly. A second, smaller run of the cuffs and earrings is planned for early 2027, and the workshop is already carving the wax. Prices for the second run will stay the same.

title: Behind the brand: the tote bag everyone in Lekki owns
excerpt: How a university side project became a waitlist of thousands.

children.text: You have seen it on the ferry, at the Lekki Conservation Centre gate and on half the laptops in any co-working space between Admiralty Way and Chevron: a heavy canvas tote, square, with a leather base and a single painted stripe across the front. It is made by Kporo, a brand that began as a final-year project at the University of Lagos in 2021.

body.caption: Kporo totes drying after their stripe is painted by hand.
body.alt: Kporo totes drying after their stripe is painted by hand.

children.text: Founders Tolu Martins and Bisola Eze were studying textile design and needed a product to cost, make and sell for a module on small business. They made forty bags from leftover canvas, sold them to classmates for ₦6,000 each, and got a B. The bags did better than the grade. Within a year, they had a waitlist they were managing on a spreadsheet.
The waitlist problem

Martins is candid that the waitlist was an accident, not a marketing plan. The pair simply could not sew faster. By 2024 there were more than four thousand names on it, and customers were reselling bags at twice the price. They responded by hiring six tailors, renting a workshop in Ajah and moving to a monthly release of 800 bags, assigned by order of sign-up.

body.quote: Scarcity looks clever from the outside. From the inside it is just people being angry at you in your DMs.

children.text: What goes into one bag

The canvas is a 16-ounce cotton duck woven in Kaduna. The leather base, which stops the bag sagging and protects it on wet floors, is cut from offcuts bought from shoemakers in Aba. Each stripe is painted by hand with fabric paint, which is why no two are identical and why the brand will not do custom colours. The bag retails for ₦32,000 and Kporo will repair the straps or replace the base for free in the first two years. The next release is on the last Saturday of October. If you are new to the list, expect to wait about two months. If you want one faster, the brand quietly sells a few seconds, bags with paint drips or uneven stitching, at its workshop on Saturdays for ₦20,000. They are, honestly, hard to tell apart.

title: Wura Knit and the Kano dye pits: a collaboration in indigo
excerpt: A Lagos knitwear label sent its undyed cotton north to Kofar Mata. What came back is the best thing either side has made.

children.text: Knitwear in Lagos sounds like a joke until you wear a loose cotton knit in an air-conditioned office and realise it was always the point. Wura Knit, run by Ijeoma Ukah from a studio in Yaba, makes open-weave cotton sweaters and vests on two second-hand flatbed machines. For autumn, Ukah wanted indigo. She went to Kano to get it.

The Kofar Mata dye pits in Kano are among the oldest still working in West Africa: deep cylindrical pits in the ground where cloth is dipped in fermented indigo, again and again, until it reaches the right shade. Ukah partnered with a family of dyers led by a woman she asked us to call Hajiya Amina, who has worked the pits for most of her life and agreed to dye knitted panels for the first time.

body.caption: Knitted panels hanging to oxidise after a dip in the Kano pits.
body.alt: Knitted panels hanging to oxidise after a dip in the Kano pits.

children.text: Knit is not like woven cloth. It stretches when wet, it holds water, and the dye can settle unevenly in the loops. The first batch came out patchy. The second came out too dark. By the fourth, Hajiya Amina had worked out that the panels needed a quicker dip, more of them, and a long rest in the shade between each one.

body.quote: She treated the knit like a new kind of child. Patient, a little suspicious, and in the end very proud of it.

children.text: The collection
Crew-neck sweater in three shades of indigo: ₦72,000
Sleeveless vest, pale indigo: ₦48,000
Short-sleeve knit shirt with tie-dyed hem: ₦56,000

Every piece is knitted in Lagos, sent north undyed, dyed by hand and returned for finishing. That journey adds two weeks and roughly ₦9,000 to each garment, which Ukah has chosen to absorb rather than pass on in full. The dye family is paid per panel and named on the label. Indigo will bleed for the first few washes. Wash it alone in cold water with a spoon of salt, dry it inside out in shade, and it settles into a colour that only gets better. The collection is in the EKPO shop from 20 October, and Wura Knit's studio on Herbert Macaulay Way has the full range.

title: Behind the brand: where the ₦28,000 goes in an Ewa Basics shirt
excerpt: A young Lagos label opened its books for us, line by line, from cotton to courier.

children.text: Ewa Basics makes one thing well: a boxy, short-sleeved cotton shirt in white, black, stone and a dusty green. It costs ₦28,000. When we asked founder Damilola Fashola why, she did something most brands will not do. She sent us the spreadsheet.

body.caption: Ewa Basics shirts being pressed before packing at the Ikeja workshop.
body.alt: Ewa Basics shirts being pressed before packing at the Ikeja workshop.

children.text: The breakdown
Here is what one shirt costs the brand to make and sell, rounded to the nearest five hundred naira and based on its September production run of 400 pieces.
Fabric (1.6 metres of Kaduna-woven cotton poplin): ₦6,500
Cutting and sewing (paid per piece to four tailors): ₦4,500
Buttons, labels, thread and packaging: ₦1,500
Workshop rent and power, shared across the run: ₦2,000
Photography, website and adverts: ₦3,000
Delivery subsidy and returns: ₦1,500
Tax and payment fees: ₦2,500
Margin left for the business: ₦6,500

That last figure is about 23 percent of the price, and it is what pays Fashola, funds the next run and covers the months when sales are slow. Fabric is the single biggest cost, and it has risen by almost a third in two years as the naira has weakened and the mills' own costs have climbed. Fashola pays herself a fixed salary of ₦350,000 a month, which she points out is less than she earned in her old job in insurance. Anything above that goes back into fabric.

body.quote: Every time someone says a Nigerian shirt should cost ₦10,000, I want to show them the power bill.

children.text: Fashola says publishing the numbers has been good for business. Customers who balk at the price usually come round once they see that the tailors are paid properly and the fabric is local. It has also made her stricter: if a cost cannot be defended in public, she cuts it. Last year that meant dropping printed tissue paper, which saved ₦300 a shirt and which nobody missed. The shirts are cut generously; most people size down. Ewa Basics sells online and from a small rail at its Ikeja workshop on Allen Avenue on Saturdays, where you can try before you buy. Returns are accepted within seven days if the shirt is unworn.

title: This week: pop-ups, gallery openings and a sample sale
excerpt: Everything worth leaving the house for in Lagos from Thursday to Sunday.

children.text: The rains are finally easing, the evenings are long again, and Lagos has packed a lot into four days. Here is what we are going to, in order, with times, prices and the one thing to know before you go.

body.caption: A print from Salt Water, opening at Hollow Room on Thursday.
body.alt: A print from Salt Water, opening at Hollow Room on Thursday.

children.text: Thursday 15 October. Hollow Room, the small gallery above a pharmacy on Adeola Odeku Street, opens Salt Water, a show of large photographs of fishing communities on the Lagos lagoon by the photographer Aniekan Udo. Udo spent three years on the water with the fishing families of the lagoon's edge, and the prints are big enough to stand inside. The opening runs from 6pm to 9pm and is free. Arrive early; the room holds about sixty people and the stairs are narrow.

Friday 16 October. Ewa Basics and Kporo share a pop-up at Atelier 9, Bourdillon Road, Ikoyi, from noon to 8pm. Expect the full colour range of Ewa shirts, a limited batch of Kporo totes in a new rust stripe, and a tailor on site doing free hemming on anything you buy. Bring cash or a transfer app; the card machine was temperamental last time.
Saturday 17 October: the big one

Lagos label Tade Osun holds its first sample sale in two years at The Annex, 3 Ajose Adeogun Street, Victoria Island, from 10am to 5pm. Pieces from the last four seasons will be priced from ₦15,000, with tailoring at around 60 percent off. The queue for the 2024 sale started at 7am, so plan accordingly.
Bring a tote: there are no bags
Fitting rooms are shared and there are only four
No returns, no exchanges
Entry is free but capped at 80 people at a time

Sunday 18 October. Slow down at the Sunday Long Table at Ìdáná, the supper-club kitchen in Surulere, from 2pm. ₦25,000 buys five courses built around corn and groundnut, plus palm wine from a tapper in Badagry. Seats go on sale on Thursday morning on the restaurant's Instagram, and there are thirty of them. Vegetarians are catered for if you say so when booking. Doing something we should know about next week? Our events desk reads every email, and the deadline for the next listing is Tuesday at noon.

title: Photos: the EKPO x Orire launch party
excerpt: Aso-oke, highlife and a queue around the block at Ikoyi.

children.text: We expected two hundred people. By 8pm there were close to five hundred, a queue that reached the end of Awolowo Road and a highlife band that agreed to play an extra hour for the price of jollof and a lift home. The EKPO x Orire capsule launched on Friday night at Gallery Lagoon in Ikoyi, and this is how it looked.

body.caption: The queue outside Gallery Lagoon, Ikoyi, shortly after doors opened.
body.alt: The queue outside Gallery Lagoon, Ikoyi, shortly after doors opened.

children.text: The collection on the night

The capsule is six pieces: a cropped chore jacket, wide trousers, a camp-collar shirt, a wrap skirt, a bucket hat and a scarf, all in an aso-oke stripe of deep green and gold woven for EKPO in Ibadan. Orire founder Morenike Adebanjo brought four of her weavers from Oke-Ado, who worked a small loom by the door all evening and handed out short lengths of cloth to anyone who asked how it was done.

body.quote: I have never seen people in Ikoyi stand still for that long to watch somebody weave. That was my favourite part.

children.text: The guest list read like a page of this magazine: designers, stylists, two of our cover stars and a large contingent of Orire customers who arrived in their own jackets from past drops. Several guests came straight from work, aso-oke jackets over office shirts, which was rather the point. The best-dressed award, unofficial and hotly debated in the EKPO group chat, went to a guest in a three-piece aso-oke suit worn with white trainers and a beaded fan.

body.caption: Weavers from Orire's Ibadan workshop demonstrating on a hand loom.
body.alt: Weavers from Orire's Ibadan workshop demonstrating on a hand loom.

children.text: The band, Eko Brass Union, played a set that leaned heavily on 1970s highlife and finished with a twelve-minute version of a song nobody could name but everyone seemed to know. Food came from Ìdáná in Surulere: small plates of ofada rice, plantain, and peppered snail on skewers that disappeared within minutes. The capsule sold out online in four hours on Saturday. Orire is also taking orders for a made-to-measure version of the jacket, with a six-week wait. A small restock of the trousers and scarves is planned for the EKPO Market in December, and the full gallery of photographs from the night is in the EKPO TV section. Thank you to everyone who queued, and our apologies to the neighbours.

title: Save the date: EKPO Market returns in December
excerpt: Sixty Nigerian brands, food from Ekpo Eats favourites and a live stage.

children.text: It is back, it is bigger, and this year it is two days. EKPO Market, our weekend of Nigerian fashion, design and food, returns on Saturday 12 and Sunday 13 December 2026 at The Yard, 14 Ozumba Mbadiwe Avenue, Victoria Island. Doors open at 11am and close at 9pm on both days.

body.caption: Shoppers at last year's EKPO Market, where the queue began before noon.
body.alt: Shoppers at last year's EKPO Market, where the queue began before noon.

children.text: Dates: Saturday 12 and Sunday 13 December 2026
Venue: The Yard, 14 Ozumba Mbadiwe Avenue, Victoria Island, Lagos
Hours: 11am to 9pm both days
Tickets: ₦5,000 per day, sold only in the EKPO shop
Children under 12 enter free with an adult

Tickets go on sale on Monday 2 November. Last year's sold out in nine days, and we have not doubled the capacity just because we have doubled the dates, so do not leave it late. Each ticket is for a single day; if you want both, buy two.

Sixty Nigerian brands have confirmed, up from thirty-eight last year, and every one of them makes its products in the country. Expect Orire Studio's full aso-oke range and the restock of the EKPO capsule, Nkem Footwear loafers in a market-only colour, Salma Ade brass, Wura Knit's indigo sweaters and Kporo totes without the waitlist. About a third of the stalls are labels we have never covered before, chosen from more than four hundred applications.

body.quote: We want people to leave having met the person who made the thing they bought. That is the whole idea.

children.text: Food and music

The food court is curated by the Ekpo Eats desk: chin chin croissants from Bake Ikeja, suya from Mallam Garba's Grill, Ìdáná's ofada bowls, and a palm wine bar run by Badagry tappers. The live stage opens at 4pm each day, with highlife on Saturday and alté and Afrobeats on Sunday. Full line-up announced in November. Every stall will take cards and transfers, there will be cash points at the gate, and the food court has covered seating for four hundred, plus a quiet room for anyone who needs a break from the crowds. Getting there: parking at The Yard is limited and costs ₦3,000. We recommend a ride-hail drop-off at the Ozumba Mbadiwe gate or the ferry to Five Cowrie terminal, a ten-minute walk away. See you in December.

title: Looking back: the first EKPO Market, December 2025
excerpt: Thirty-eight brands, one very hot afternoon and a lot of lessons. What we learned from our first market.

children.text: Eight months ago, we put thirty-eight Nigerian brands under canvas in a car park in Victoria Island and hoped someone would come. About four thousand people did. As we start planning the next one, here is an honest look back at the first EKPO Market.

body.caption: The opening hour of the first EKPO Market, December 2025.
body.alt: The opening hour of the first EKPO Market, December 2025.

children.text: What worked? The brands, first of all. Every stall was a label that makes in Nigeria, and many were selling face to face for the first time. Nkem Footwear sold out of loafers by 3pm. Kporo brought 200 totes and left with eleven. Several designers told us afterwards that the market was their best single day of the year, and two of them met the manufacturers they now work with at neighbouring stalls. The food worked too. The Ekpo Eats court, eight vendors in a ring around a shaded seating area, became the social centre of the day. The suya queue was its own event.
What did not
Shade: there was not enough, and the 2pm sun was brutal
Card payments: the network dropped twice and several stalls lost sales
Toilets: four was not enough for four thousand people
Exit: one gate in and out made the end of the day slow

We heard about all of these, often loudly, and we deserved it. Fixing them is the main reason this year's market moves to a new venue with covered areas, a dedicated internet line for traders, and separate entrance and exit gates.

body.quote: We sold more in six hours than in the previous two months online. But I also got sunburnt for the first time in my life.

children.text: The plan for December 2026 is a two-day market with sixty brands, a live stage and more seats in the food court. Ticket prices will go up modestly, to cover the bigger site, and every stall fee will remain flat so smaller labels are not priced out. Details will be announced in October. Thank you to everyone who came, queued, complained and came back to tell us it was worth it. If you were there and have a story, a photo or a complaint we have not yet heard, our events desk would still like to hear it.

title: Photos: Adire Night at a Yaba warehouse
excerpt: Twelve dyers, one indigo vat and a dance floor that never quite dried. Our photographers were there.

children.text: Most parties do not come with a warning to wear clothes you do not mind ruining. Adire Night did, and almost everyone ignored it. On Saturday, the collective Indigo Commons took over a disused bakery warehouse off Herbert Macaulay Way in Yaba for an evening that was half workshop, half dance party and entirely blue.

body.caption: Guests tying cloth before their first dip in the indigo vat.
body.alt: Guests tying cloth before their first dip in the indigo vat.

children.text: The ticket, ₦12,000, came with a plain white cotton scarf. At one end of the warehouse, twelve dyers from Abeokuta ran tables where guests could tie, stitch or wax their scarf with simple patterns, then dip it in a large indigo vat under supervision. The scarves were hung on lines across the room to oxidise, turning from green to deep blue as the night went on, so that by midnight the ceiling was a canopy of drying cloth.

body.quote: Indigo is a living thing. You can only rush it so much, so you might as well dance while you wait.

children.text: At the other end, a sound system played a long set from DJ Kemi Lux that moved from fuji to amapiano to old highlife records. Between the two, there was a bar serving zobo cocktails, and a long trestle table selling finished adire from the dyers' own workshops at prices from ₦8,000 for a scarf to ₦45,000 for a full wrapper.

body.caption: Finished scarves drying above the dance floor around midnight.
body.alt: Finished scarves drying above the dance floor around midnight.

children.text: A grandmother from Abeokuta teaching a group of teenagers the oniko tie technique
The moment the first scarves turned blue and the room applauded
Blue fingerprints on every glass at the bar by 11pm
Guests leaving at 2am still holding their damp scarves like trophies

Indigo Commons says it plans to hold Adire Night every quarter, with the next one in January. Tickets for this one sold out in two days, and the collective says it will cap numbers at three hundred again to keep the queue for the vat manageable. Ticket sales will be announced on its Instagram. Our advice for next time: wear dark clothes, bring a plastic bag for the ride home, and do not touch your face.

title: A year of EKPO Supper Clubs, in twelve dinners
excerpt: From a rooftop in Surulere to a fishing village in Badagry: every table we laid, and the one we would do again tomorrow.

children.text: Last September we invited twenty-four readers to dinner on a rooftop in Surulere, cooked by a chef we had been writing about for months. It was meant to be a one-off. Twelve months and twelve dinners later, the EKPO Supper Club has fed nearly four hundred people, and this is a look back at all of them.

body.caption: The long table at the Badagry supper, laid on the sand at sunset.
body.alt: The long table at the Badagry supper, laid on the sand at sunset.

children.text: Each dinner is hosted by a different cook, held somewhere that is not a restaurant, and limited to between twenty and forty guests. Tickets have ranged from ₦20,000 to ₦45,000, depending on the menu, and all of the profit goes to the cook. Guests sit at a single long table and are seated next to people they did not arrive with. That last rule was unpopular at first and is now the thing people mention most.
Our favourites
October: a seven-course Efik dinner in a Calabar family compound, cooked by three generations of the same family
January: grilled croaker and coconut rice on the beach at a fishing village near Badagry
March: an all-vegetable menu by chef Nonso Eke in a plant nursery in Ikeja
June: a Hausa breakfast feast, at 7am, in a courtyard in Kaduna
August: a dessert-only night in a Lekki bakery after closing time

body.quote: I cooked for strangers in my grandmother's compound, and by the end they were washing dishes with my aunties. That is the night I will remember.
body.cite: Ekaete Bassey, host of the Calabar supper

children.text: Not every dinner was a triumph. A rooftop in Ikoyi lost power halfway through the main course and we finished by phone torchlight. In February we overbooked by six and squeezed in a second table that wobbled all night. We have learned to bring a generator, a spare table and more ice than seems reasonable.

Two hosts have since used their supper club takings to open small kitchens of their own, which is the best review we could ask for. The supper club continues in November with a dinner in Port Harcourt built around the city's seafood, and we are taking it to Abuja for the first time early next year. Newsletter subscribers hear about tickets first, and they usually go within a day. Vegetarian and allergy-friendly menus can be arranged for every dinner if you tell us when you book.

title: How to wear an agbada to the office
excerpt: Keep the volume, lose the formality: three ways to style it for work.

children.text: The agbada is built for arrival. Three pieces, metres of cloth, sleeves you fold over your shoulders like wings. It is the outfit for weddings, chieftaincy titles and the front row of a funeral. It is also, worn the right way, one of the most comfortable things you can put on for a long day at a desk. The secret is to treat it as separates. Most people own the full set and only wear it together. Break it up and you get a wide outer robe that works like a coat, a long tunic that works like a shirt, and trousers that are cooler than anything in your wardrobe.

body.caption: A cotton agbada worn open over a plain tee and tailored trousers.
body.alt: A cotton agbada worn open over a plain tee and tailored trousers.

children.text: Three looks for work

Look one: the robe as a coat. Take the outer robe of a lightweight agbada, cotton or linen rather than damask, and wear it open over a plain white or black T-shirt and slim tailored trousers. Push the sleeves up to the elbow. Finish with loafers or clean leather trainers. This is the easiest of the three and the one that turns the most heads in a lift.

Look two: tunic and trousers only. Leave the robe at home. The inner tunic, the buba, worn with its matching trousers, is essentially a long, relaxed suit. Choose a muted colour, stone, navy or olive, and keep the embroidery minimal. Add a structured bag and a good watch. On Friday, swap the trousers for dark jeans.

Look three: the full set, dressed down. If your workplace is relaxed or you have a presentation to give, wear all three pieces, but in a single quiet colour with no embroidery and no cap. Fold the sleeves neatly on the shoulders rather than letting them hang. Sandals with a closed back, not slides.

body.quote: The agbada was always work clothing. Kings worked. Traders worked. It is only recently we decided it was a costume.

children.text: Fabric: cotton, linen or a light guinea brocade, never heavy damask
Fit: the tunic should sit just above the knee
Colour: one colour head to toe looks most modern
Cost: a made-to-measure cotton set starts around ₦60,000 from a good tailor

title: Caring for adire so it lasts decades
excerpt: Wash cold, dry in shade, and other advice from Abeokuta dyers.

children.text: Good adire gets better with age. The indigo settles, the blues soften and the cloth becomes as comfortable as an old shirt. Bad care, on the other hand, can strip it to a dull grey in a single season. We spent an afternoon with the dyers of the Itoku market in Abeokuta to learn how to keep it looking right.

body.caption: Adire drying in the shade at a dyer's compound in Itoku, Abeokuta.
body.alt: Adire drying in the shade at a dyer's compound in Itoku, Abeokuta.

children.text: New adire will bleed. This is not a fault; it is excess dye that has not bonded with the cotton. Wash a new piece on its own, by hand, in a basin of cold water with a tablespoon of salt and a few drops of mild soap. Leave it to soak for fifteen minutes, swish it gently, rinse until the water runs nearly clear, and do not wring it.

body.quote: Treat it the way you treat your hair. Gentle soap, cold water, no hard rubbing, and never leave it in the sun to roast.

children.text: Everyday care
Always wash cold. Hot water lifts indigo fast.
Use mild soap. Skip bleach and any detergent that promises brightening.
Turn it inside out before washing to protect the surface.
Dry in the shade. Direct Lagos sun will fade it in weeks.
Iron on a medium heat, on the reverse, while slightly damp.
Do not dry-clean starched or cassava-paste adire; the chemicals attack the resist pattern.
If you must use a washing machine, use the cold, delicate cycle, put the piece in a mesh bag, and wash it only with other dark clothes. Expect a little more fading over time.

If an old piece has gone pale, you can have it re-dipped. Most dyers in Itoku and in Lagos markets such as Oshodi will re-dye a wrapper for between ₦4,000 and ₦8,000, depending on the size and how deep you want the colour. The pattern will soften slightly, which many people prefer. Small holes can be darned with dark cotton thread by any good tailor and, on a busy pattern, are almost invisible. Store adire folded in a drawer away from light, with a bar of local black soap or a few cloves to keep insects away. Looked after this way, a good piece will outlive whoever buys it.

title: The buying guide: tailored trousers under ₦40,000
excerpt: Where to find a well-cut pair, and what to look for when you do.

children.text: A good pair of trousers does more work than almost anything else you own. It goes to the office, to dinner, to a wedding with the right shirt. And in Lagos you do not need to spend a fortune on one. Here is what to check, and where we have found the best value this year.
Fabric: run your hand along it. Good wool blends and cotton twills feel dense and spring back when squeezed.
Waistband: should be lined and have a hook as well as a button.
Seams: there should be at least two centimetres of spare fabric at the back seam for letting out later.
Pockets: deep, lined with cotton not polyester, and sewn shut on a new pair.
Hem: unfinished or generous. A short hem cannot be fixed.

body.caption: A pleated cotton twill trouser from Ola Tailoring, ₦34,000.
body.alt: A pleated cotton twill trouser from Ola Tailoring, ₦34,000.

children.text: As for where to buy, start with Ola Tailoring, in a small shop off Opebi Road in Ikeja, makes ready-to-wear trousers in three cuts, straight, tapered and a wide pleated style, in cotton twill and a light wool blend. Prices run from ₦28,000 to ₦38,000 and they will hem on the spot. The pleated twill is our favourite pair of the year.

Afolabi and Sons, a third-generation tailoring stall in Balogun Market, will make a pair to measure for ₦25,000 plus fabric. Bring your own or buy from the cloth sellers two rows over. Allow a week and go back for a fitting. If you prefer something ready-made and fast, Ewa Basics has started selling a drawstring trouser in cotton canvas for ₦30,000. It is more relaxed than true tailoring, but the cut is clean and it holds a crease.

body.quote: Buy for the hips and the seat. Everything else, a tailor can fix in twenty minutes.

children.text: The fit, in one minute

Stand up straight. The waistband should sit flat without pulling. There should be no horizontal creases across the front when you stand, and no sagging fabric under the seat. When you sit, the waist should not dig in. And the hem should just touch your shoe, with a single small break. Anything more is a ₦2,000 job for your tailor.

title: Five fixes your tailor can make for under ₦5,000
excerpt: Small alterations that make old clothes look brand new.

children.text: Before you buy anything new this season, open your wardrobe and look for the clothes you never wear because something is slightly off. Often it is a five-minute job. We took a pile of our own neglected clothes to Mr Sunday Okon, who runs a busy alteration stall at the corner of Ogunlana Drive in Surulere, and asked what he would fix and for how much.

body.caption: Mr Sunday Okon at work at his alteration stall in Surulere.
body.alt: Mr Sunday Okon at work at his alteration stall in Surulere.

children.text: He has been altering clothes from the same corner for twenty-two years, under a faded umbrella, with a treadle machine he still prefers to the electric one his son bought him. He looked at our pile for about a minute, sorted it into two heaps, and told us that almost everything in the bigger one could be saved for less than the price of a taxi home.
The five fixes

1. Taking in a shirt at the sides. Most ready-made shirts are cut boxy to fit as many bodies as possible. Taking two or three centimetres off each side seam makes a shirt look made for you. ₦2,500 to ₦3,500.

2. Shortening sleeves. A shirt sleeve should end at the base of your thumb; on a jacket, a little shirt cuff should show. Plain sleeves cost around ₦2,000. Jacket sleeves with working buttons cost more and are best left to a specialist.
3. Tapering trousers. Wide legs are back, but if yours flap at the ankle, a gentle taper from the knee down gives a cleaner line. ₦3,000 to ₦4,000.

4. Replacing buttons. Cheap plastic buttons make good fabric look cheap. Swapping them for horn, wood or corozo can transform a shirt or coat. Labour is about ₦1,000; buttons from the haberdashery stalls at Tejuosho Market cost ₦100 to ₦500 each.
5. Fixing a hem. A hem that has dropped, or trousers that pool at your shoes, are the fastest fix of all. ₦1,500 to ₦2,000, usually done while you wait.

body.quote: People throw away clothes that only need ten minutes of my time. Bring them to me first, then throw them away if I say no.

children.text: Two pieces of advice from Mr Okon: always try the garment on in front of your tailor so they can pin it on your body, and never let anyone cut fabric they cannot put back. A tailor who says a job is impossible is often the one worth trusting.

title: How to wear one ankara two-piece five ways
excerpt: A matching shirt and trouser set is the hardest-working outfit you own, if you stop wearing it only as a set.

children.text: Almost everyone in Nigeria has one: a matching ankara shirt and trousers, made for a wedding, an owambe or a family photograph, then hung up and forgotten. The print is loud and the set feels like a costume. But split it into its two halves and it becomes two of the most useful pieces in your wardrobe.
We styled a single set, a blue-and-ochre wax print from a tailor in Ojota, five ways over one working week.

body.caption: One ankara set, five outfits: our stylist's working week.
body.alt: One ankara set, five outfits: our stylist's working week.

children.text: One set, Monday to Friday

Monday: the shirt, toned down. Wear it with plain navy or charcoal trousers and dark leather shoes. Pull one colour from the print, here the navy, and keep everything else in it. The print reads as a statement rather than a uniform.

Tuesday: the trousers, with white. Pair them with a crisp white shirt or tee, and nothing else patterned. White calms any print and makes the trousers look deliberate rather than borrowed from a party.
Wednesday: layered. Wear the shirt open over a fitted black tee, with black jeans. This is the most relaxed version and the best one for a long day in traffic.

Thursday: under a jacket. Button the shirt under a plain unstructured blazer in stone or olive, so only the collar and a strip of print show. It looks like you planned your outfit for a week, which in fairness you did.

Friday: the full set, dressed down. Finally, wear it together, but with clean white trainers instead of formal shoes and the shirt untucked. The set looks younger and far less like you are on your way to a reception.

By the end of the week, two colleagues had asked where the shirt was from and nobody had noticed it was the same one every day. That is the real test of a print: whether it can become part of your ordinary week rather than something saved for the photographer at somebody else's wedding.

body.quote: The trick with print is to give it room. One loud thing at a time, and it never looks like too much.

children.text: Keep a plain navy, white and black piece on hand to balance the print
Choose shoes in a colour pulled from the print
Iron the print side down to stop the wax finish going shiny
If the set is too snug to split comfortably, a tailor can let it out for about ₦3,000

title: The buying guide: a harmattan jacket for ₦60,000 or less
excerpt: Dust, cold mornings and hot afternoons. Here is what to buy before November, and where to find it.

children.text: Harmattan is coming. In Lagos it means hazy, cool mornings and dusty afternoons; further north it means genuinely cold dawns, cracked lips and a fine coat of sand on everything. Either way, a single light jacket is the most useful thing you can buy this month. Here is what to look for and five we would happily spend our money on.
Tightly woven cotton or canvas that keeps dust out but lets you breathe
No lining, or a thin cotton one; you will be taking it off by noon
Dark or mid colours that hide dust
Pockets that close, for your phone and keys
Machine-washable, because it will need washing every week

body.caption: Five harmattan jackets under ₦60,000, photographed in Yaba.
body.alt: Five harmattan jackets under ₦60,000, photographed in Yaba.

children.text: Our five picks

Orire Studio's aso-oke chore jacket is above budget, but its unlined cotton overshirt at ₦58,000 uses the same cloth and is the best-looking piece on this list. It comes in indigo and a warm brown. Kanvas Lab, a small workshop in Kaduna, makes a hooded canvas jacket for ₦45,000 in olive and black, with deep zip pockets and a drawstring hem. Ideal if you are travelling north.

Ewa Basics has an overshirt in heavy cotton for ₦38,000. Simple, square and sized generously enough to wear over a knit. For something lighter, Wura Knit's indigo cardigan, ₦52,000, blocks the morning chill and packs flat in a bag for the afternoon. And at Yaba Market, the secondhand stalls behind the main bend reliably have old workwear and denim jackets for ₦8,000 to ₦20,000. Wash before wearing and ask the trader to replace any missing buttons on the spot.

body.quote: Buy one that you can stuff in a bag at 1pm. If you cannot, it is a winter coat and this is not winter.

children.text: A final tip: harmattan dust is fine and gets into everything. Shake your jacket out every evening and wash it at least once a week, cold, to keep the colour. And if the dust gets to your skin as well as your clothes, shea butter from any market stall, about ₦1,500 a tub, does more than anything in a pharmacy.

title: Ekpo's Guide to Lagos: a weekend in Surulere
excerpt: Vintage shops, suya spots and the best rooftop bar on the mainland.

children.text: Surulere does not try to impress you, which is exactly why it does. The old heart of mainland Lagos, home to the National Stadium and generations of footballers, musicians and market women, rewards anyone willing to walk its side streets slowly. Here is how we would spend a weekend there.

On Saturday, shop. Start at Bend Down Vintage, a narrow shop on Adelabu Street stacked to the ceiling with secondhand denim, football shirts and 1990s Nigerian print shirts. Prices start at ₦3,000 and everything is negotiable after noon. Ask for the old national team jerseys, which appear every few weeks and vanish within hours. Two streets away, Ojuolape Records sells highlife and juju vinyl from crates on the floor; ask the owner to play before you buy. Lunch is at Iya Bisi's Buka on Bode Thomas Street: order the ofada rice with ayamase, ₦3,500, and a cold zobo. Get there before 1pm or the stew runs out.

body.caption: Crates of highlife vinyl at Ojuolape Records, Surulere.
body.alt: Crates of highlife vinyl at Ojuolape Records, Surulere.

children.text: On Saturday night, go up. The best rooftop on the mainland is The Ledge, on the seventh floor of an office block on Adeniran Ogunsanya Street. It is unpretentious, with plastic chairs, strong breeze and a view across the stadium to the lagoon. Order the chapman, ₦4,000, and the peppered gizzard. Thursday to Saturday a DJ plays old Fela and new Afrobeats in about equal measure.

body.quote: People come for the view and stay for the music. The view is free; the music is my brother.

children.text: Sunday: slow
Breakfast: akara and pap from the stall at the corner of Ishaga Road, ₦1,500, from 7am
Late morning: a walk around the stadium grounds, where Sunday football runs all day
Afternoon: Ìdáná supper club's Sunday Long Table, booked in advance, from ₦25,000
Evening: suya from Mallam Garba's Grill on Ojuelegba Road; ask for the ram, extra yaji

Getting around: Surulere is best on foot or by short okada hops. Leave the car at your hotel or arrive by BRT to Ojuelegba, and keep cash on you for the smaller stalls. If you want to stay over, Bode Thomas Guest House is clean, quiet and about ₦35,000 a night, with a breakfast of yam and egg sauce included.

title: Ekpo's Guide to Abuja: where to shop in Wuse
excerpt: Designer boutiques, tailors, and a fabric market you will want a whole morning for.

children.text: Abuja has a reputation for being polished and a little quiet. Wuse, its busiest commercial district, is neither. Between the market, the boutiques of Wuse 2 and the tailoring workshops tucked behind them, it is the best place in the capital to spend money on clothes. Here is where we go.

body.caption: Bolts of brocade and lace at Wuse Market, Abuja.
body.alt: Bolts of brocade and lace at Wuse Market, Abuja.

children.text: Give Wuse Market a whole morning. The fabric section, deep in the covered halls, has everything from Swiss voile and Austrian lace to guinea brocade and northern hand-woven cloth. Our favourite stall is Alhaji Bashir's, row F, where a five-yard length of good brocade costs ₦25,000 to ₦45,000 and the family will tell you honestly which bolts are local and which are imported. Bargain, politely. Go early; by noon the halls are hot and crowded. If you want a complete outfit, the tailors listed below can work from anything you buy here, and the family will happily point you to the right one.

Then head to Wuse 2. Along Aminu Kano Crescent and the streets off it you will find most of Abuja's independent designers. Studio Zaria sells tailored kaftans in raw silk from ₦95,000 and is worth visiting for the fitting room alone, a cool, quiet space at the back of the shop. Neem, two doors down, stocks small-batch labels from Kano and Kaduna, including the hooded canvas jackets from Kanvas Lab.

body.quote: Abuja customers know fabric. You cannot sell them polyester and call it silk. They will touch it and laugh.

children.text: The tailors
Hassan Couture, behind Banex Plaza: kaftans and babban riga made to measure from ₦30,000 plus fabric, one week
Madam Grace Alterations, Wuse Zone 4: fast and precise fixes from ₦1,500
Shehu Embroidery, Wuse Market back gate: hand embroidery on collars and cuffs from ₦8,000

Break for lunch at Kilishi House on Adetokunbo Ademola Crescent, where a plate of tuwo shinkafa with miyan taushe costs ₦4,500 and the kilishi to take home is sold by weight. Taxi drivers know every place on this list, and most rides within Wuse cost under ₦2,000. Many shops close for a few hours around Friday prayers, so Thursday or Saturday is the better day for a long shopping trip.

title: Ekpo's Guide to Port Harcourt: after dark
excerpt: Live music, late food and the clubs locals actually go to.

children.text: Port Harcourt nights start late and end later. The Garden City has a live music scene that rivals Lagos, a street food culture built around the sea, and a crowd that dresses up even on a Tuesday. Here is a night out, hour by hour, the way people who live there would plan it.

body.caption: The band at Ofo Lounge, Old GRA, warming up before midnight.
body.alt: The band at Ofo Lounge, Old GRA, warming up before midnight.

children.text: The night, hour by hour

At 9pm, eat first. Start at Mama Ibiere's Fish Spot, a row of charcoal grills on a quiet street in D-Line. Choose your fish from the cool box, catfish, croaker or the prized tilapia from Bonny, and it comes back grilled with a fierce pepper sauce and boiled yam. A whole fish for two costs around ₦12,000. Pair it with a cold drink from the kiosk next door and do not wear white. The grills light up at 7pm and the best fish is usually gone by ten.

At 11pm, move on to live music. Ofo Lounge, in a converted colonial bungalow in Old GRA, has a house band that plays Rivers highlife and Ijaw owigiri four nights a week, with guest singers on Fridays. Entry is ₦5,000 and the garden fills up fast. Order the palm wine served in calabash, ₦3,000, and the periwinkle pepper soup if you are still hungry. Tables near the stage are first come, first served, and nobody minds if you dance in the aisle.

body.quote: We play the songs your grandparents danced to, just louder. Port Harcourt has always been a music city.

children.text: By 1am, it is time to dance. The club the locals actually go to is Basement 22, under a shopping plaza on Aba Road. It is dark, loud and uninterested in VIP tables, and the DJs play amapiano, Afrobeats and a surprising amount of old-school Port Harcourt rap. Entry is ₦10,000 on Fridays and Saturdays. Dress sharp but sensibly: the stairs down are steep and the floor is concrete, so leave the highest heels at home.
Late snack: bole and fish from the stalls near Rumuola junction, open until 3am
Getting home: use a ride-hail app, not street taxis, and share your trip
Dress code: smart; Port Harcourt dresses up
Cash: keep some, as card machines in smaller spots are unreliable

title: Ekpo's Guide to Calabar: beyond the carnival
excerpt: Quiet cafes, craft markets and where to eat edikang ikong.

children.text: Every December, Calabar is the centre of Nigeria's party calendar. For the other eleven months, it is something else: a calm, green, clean city on the Calabar River, with hills, old colonial buildings and some of the best cooking in the country. This guide is for the quiet season, when the city is easy to walk and the cooks have time to talk.

Begin your morning at Cafe Atakpa, a small cafe in a restored wooden house near the Marina, where the coffee comes from the Obudu plateau and the plantain bread is baked each morning. A cup and a slice costs ₦3,500. From there, walk the old colonial quarter up the hill towards Duke Town, where the streets are lined with wooden-balconied houses and mango trees. Wear flat shoes; the hill is steeper than it looks.

body.caption: A wooden-balconied house in Duke Town, Calabar.
body.alt: A wooden-balconied house in Duke Town, Calabar.

children.text: In the afternoon, go to the markets. Watt Market is the city's big, busy market and the place to buy the dried fish, crayfish and fresh leaves that make Efik cooking what it is. For crafts, go to Ekpe Craft House on Mary Slessor Avenue, a cooperative of makers selling raffia bags from ₦6,000, carved wooden spoons, beaded jewellery and woven ukara cloth, priced fairly with the maker's name on every tag. Haggling at Watt is expected; at Ekpe Craft House the prices are fixed, and the makers are often there to talk about their work.

body.quote: Visitors come for the carnival and do not see us. Come in March and we will cook for you properly.

children.text: Evenings: eat

Edikang Kitchen, in a family house near the University of Calabar, is the place for edikang ikong, the rich vegetable soup of ugu and waterleaf with periwinkle and meat. Order it with pounded yam, ₦5,500, and ask whether the afang is ready that day. Bookings are by phone only and essential at weekends. Dessert is simple and perfect: fresh pineapple or a slice of coconut cake.
Also eat: ekpang nkukwo, the cocoyam and leaf dish, best at Edikang Kitchen on Sundays
Also drink: fresh palm wine at the bar by the Marina, before 6pm when it is sweetest
Also see: the riverfront at sunset, best from the old Marina jetty

title: Ekpo's Guide to Lagos: Yaba on ₦20,000
excerpt: Thrift stalls, cheap and excellent food, and a bookshop with a garden. A full day in Yaba without breaking the bank.

children.text: Yaba is where Lagos goes to be young: tech start-ups, two universities, the city's best thrift market and food that is cheap because the customers are students. With ₦20,000 and a free Saturday, here is how we spent a day there, with every naira accounted for.

body.caption: Saturday morning at the thrift stalls of Yaba Market.
body.alt: Saturday morning at the thrift stalls of Yaba Market.

children.text: The day, in order

We started at 9am at Yaba Market's secondhand section, known to everyone as Okrika, before the heat and crowds arrived. Our haul: a 1990s denim jacket for ₦7,000 and a striped cotton shirt for ₦2,500, both after friendly bargaining. Tip: carry small notes, inspect seams in daylight, and walk the whole market before you buy anything. Look out for labels from old Nigerian garment factories, which turn up more often than you would think and are usually better made than the imports around them. By 11am we needed food. Mama Toyin's, a small canteen near the Yaba bus stop, served us a plate of amala with ewedu and gbegiri, plus a piece of beef, for ₦2,500. It was the best meal of the day.

Early afternoon was spent at Pagekeepers, a secondhand bookshop on Commercial Avenue with a small garden at the back. Novels are ₦1,000 to ₦3,000 and you can read in the garden as long as you like. We bought a battered 1980s paperback novel for ₦2,000 and a zobo for ₦500. The owner runs a free reading club in the garden on the first Saturday of every month.

body.quote: Students have no money and very good taste. If you can sell to Yaba, you can sell to anyone.

children.text: Thrift jacket and shirt: ₦9,500
Lunch at Mama Toyin's: ₦2,500
Book and zobo at Pagekeepers: ₦2,500
Puff-puff and coffee at Yaba Grind: ₦2,000
Okada and BRT fares for the day: ₦2,500
Left over: ₦1,000 for the ride home

We finished at Yaba Grind, a coffee bar in a converted shipping container near the Herbert Macaulay Way roundabout, where a cappuccino and a bag of warm puff-puff cost ₦2,000 together. Total spent: ₦19,000. Not bad for a full day out in Lagos. Next time, we might skip the book and spend it on a second plate of amala.

title: Ekpo's Guide to Port Harcourt: a Saturday in Old GRA
excerpt: Tree-lined streets, a tailor who does it all, and the best seafood brunch in the Garden City.

children.text: Old GRA is Port Harcourt at its most graceful: wide streets shaded by flame trees, colonial-era bungalows turned into cafes and studios, and a slower pace than the rest of the city. If you have one daytime Saturday in the Garden City, spend it here.

Start with brunch. Tide Table, on Forces Avenue, serves the brunch everyone in Port Harcourt talks about. Order the seafood okpa, a steamed bambara-nut cake topped with prawns and crayfish, ₦7,500, and the plantain pancakes with palm sugar syrup, ₦5,000. Sit on the veranda, not inside; the ceiling fans out there are better than any air conditioner. Arrive before 10am on Saturdays; after that, the wait for a veranda table can stretch to forty minutes, though the staff will bring you a glass of cold zobo while you stand.

body.caption: Seafood okpa on the veranda at Tide Table, Old GRA.
body.alt: Seafood okpa on the veranda at Tide Table, Old GRA.

children.text: A short walk away is Ibinabo Atelier, a tailoring studio in a converted garage, run by Ibinabo George, who makes George wrappers into sharp shirts, bomber jackets and wide trousers. Made-to-measure shirts start at ₦40,000 plus fabric, and she keeps a rail of ready-made pieces for visitors who cannot wait. Fittings take about twenty minutes, and she will post finished pieces to Lagos or Abuja for ₦5,000. Next door, Riverine Goods stocks Niger Delta crafts: woven mats, brass bangles and bottles of local honey from Bayelsa.

body.quote: George cloth is for chiefs and weddings, yes, but it is also just very beautiful fabric. Why only wear it twice a year?

children.text: Before you leave
Walk Forces Avenue end to end for the old bungalows and the shade
Buy plantain chips and roasted groundnuts from the sellers along the Forces Avenue roadside
Visit Kiln, a small ceramics studio on Ikwerre Road, open Saturdays from 11am, with mugs from ₦6,000
Get to the waterfront by 5pm if you want fresh periwinkle for dinner

Old GRA is compact and walkable, but the sun is strong after 11am. Bring water, a hat, and a little patience for the traffic out of the neighbourhood at the end of the day. Most of the places here close by 6pm, so this is a daytime plan; for the night, see our Port Harcourt after-dark guide.

title: The Lagos restaurants we keep going back to
excerpt: Twelve kitchens, from bukas to tasting menus, ranked by how often we return.

children.text: This is not a list of the best restaurants in Lagos. It is a list of the ones we actually go back to, counted honestly from the EKPO team's bank statements and group chat over the past year. Some are expensive. Most are not. All of them are places we would send a friend tonight.

body.caption: Lunchtime at Iya Bisi's Buka, our most-visited kitchen of the year.
body.alt: Lunchtime at Iya Bisi's Buka, our most-visited kitchen of the year.

children.text: The top six
1. Iya Bisi's Buka, Surulere: ofada rice and ayamase, ₦3,500. We went 41 times.
2. Mallam Garba's Grill, Ojuelegba: ram suya with extra yaji, ₦5,000 a portion.
3. Ìdáná, Surulere: the Sunday Long Table, from ₦25,000, booked weeks ahead.
4. Mama Toyin's, Yaba: amala, ewedu and gbegiri, ₦2,500.
5. Bake Ikeja, Ikeja GRA: chin chin croissants, ₦1,800, before 9am.
6. Lekki Fish Shack, Lekki Phase 1: whole grilled croaker for two, ₦18,000.
The next six
7. Asun Corner, Ikoyi: peppered goat and cold beer, ₦6,000.
8. Tabula, Victoria Island: the seven-course tasting menu, ₦85,000, for big occasions.
9. Edikaiko House, Ikeja: Efik soups, best on Fridays.
10. Noodle Bar 23, Lekki: indomie elevated, ₦4,500, and better than it sounds.
11. Kwara Kitchen, Ilupeju: ofada and pounded yam, ₦4,000.
12. Akara Aunty, Obalende: hot akara in paper at 7am, ₦1,000.

body.quote: We do not change the menu because the customers would riot. Same ayamase since 1998.
body.cite: Iya Bisi, owner, Iya Bisi's Buka

children.text: What the top of the list has in common is consistency. The ayamase at Iya Bisi's is the same every time, the suya at Mallam Garba's is always ready by 7pm, and nobody at either place has ever rushed us out. The tasting menu at Tabula is extraordinary, but you go twice a year, not twice a week. The list rewards places that feel like part of your week, and that is exactly how we wanted it. Prices are what we paid in September and will almost certainly have gone up by the time you read this. Most of the bukas take transfers now, but carry cash in case the network fails. Tell us where you keep going back to. If enough readers name the same place, we will go and eat there, and it might make next year's list.

title: Recipe: a weekday afang soup
excerpt: A faster version of the Efik classic, ready in under an hour.

children.text: Afang is the soup my mother made for Sunday lunch and big occasions, and it is a project: pounding the leaves, simmering the meat for hours, picking periwinkles out one by one. This weekday version, adapted with help from Calabar cook Nkoyo Effiong, takes shortcuts that do not show. It serves four and is ready in about fifty minutes.

body.caption: Weekday afang soup with pounded yam.
body.alt: Weekday afang soup with pounded yam.

children.text: Ingredients
500g beef or goat, cut small so it cooks fast
200g shaki (tripe), pre-cooked
1 cup pre-shredded afang leaves (okazi), from the market or frozen
4 large handfuls waterleaf, chopped
1 cup cleaned periwinkles
1 medium dried fish, deboned and flaked
3 tablespoons ground crayfish
1 cup palm oil
2 scotch bonnet peppers, blended
2 stock cubes and salt to taste
Method
1. Season the meat with stock cubes, salt and half the pepper. Cook in a little water for 20 minutes, until nearly tender. Add the shaki for the last 5 minutes.
2. Add the dried fish, periwinkle and crayfish. Simmer for 5 minutes.
3. Pound or blend the afang leaves for a few seconds; they should be crushed, not puréed.
4. Add the waterleaf and cook for 3 minutes, until it releases its water.
5. Pour in the palm oil and stir. Cover and simmer for 5 minutes.
6. Add the afang and remaining pepper, stir well and cook for 3 to 4 minutes only. Taste for salt and serve at once.

body.quote: The waterleaf is the water. If you add water to afang, you have made a different soup.

children.text: Two notes. First, do not overcook the afang; it should stay bright green and slightly firm. Second, the soup thickens as it rests, so if you make it the night before, warm it slowly and do not add water. Serve with pounded yam, garri or fufu. The full ingredients will cost around ₦15,000 at a Lagos market this month, and it feeds four with leftovers. If you cannot find fresh periwinkle, frozen works, or leave it out and add extra dried fish. Shredded afang leaves dry out quickly, so use them within a day of buying or freeze them in small portions.

title: Meet the baker selling out of chin chin croissants
excerpt: Every morning at 7am, and gone by 9.

children.text: At 6:45 on a Tuesday morning there are already eleven people outside a small shopfront on a quiet street in Ikeja GRA. Nobody is talking. Everybody is looking at the door. At 7am it opens, and Temi Ogunleye, owner and only baker at Bake Ikeja, starts selling the pastry that made her briefly famous: the chin chin croissant.

body.caption: Chin chin croissants cooling at Bake Ikeja, minutes before opening.
body.alt: Chin chin croissants cooling at Bake Ikeja, minutes before opening.

children.text: It is exactly what it sounds like. A properly laminated butter croissant, rolled in a crunchy coating of crushed chin chin, the fried sweet dough snack every Nigerian child has eaten from a bag at a party, and finished with a glaze flavoured with nutmeg. It costs ₦1,800, and she makes 240 a day. By about 8:45 they are gone.
From accountant to baker

Ogunleye trained as an accountant and baked as a hobby until 2023, when she took a short pastry course in Accra and came home determined to make croissants in a city where butter melts on the counter. The early batches were a disaster. She solved the heat by laminating the dough at 4am, the coolest part of the day, in a room cooled with two industrial air conditioners she bought with her savings. It took almost a year of failed batches before she was happy enough to sell one.

body.quote: Lagos is the worst city in the world to make croissants, so I knew if I could do it here, I could do it anywhere.

children.text: The chin chin version came from her nephew, who asked her to put his favourite snack on top. She posted a picture, it was shared across Lagos within a day, and the queue has been there ever since. She has resisted opening a second shop or taking pre-orders, insisting she would rather make fewer pastries well than more badly. On weekends that nephew, now nineteen, works the till, and he will tell anyone who asks that the whole thing was his idea.
Opens: Tuesday to Sunday, 7am until sold out
Also try: the zobo and ginger danish, ₦2,000, and the plain croissant, ₦1,200
Order limit: six per person
Tip: weekdays are calmer; Saturdays sell out by 8am

title: Suya, rated: we tried twenty spots so you do not have to
excerpt: Our tasting panel's verdict on the city's best grilled meat.

children.text: Over four weeks, a tasting panel of five EKPO staff ate suya from twenty grills across Lagos, from Ojuelegba to Lekki, at least twice each. We ordered beef and, where available, ram and kidney, always with yaji and onions, and always after dark when the grills are hottest. We marked each spot out of ten for meat, spice, char and value. Here is what we found.

body.caption: Ram suya on the grill at Mallam Garba's, Ojuelegba.
body.alt: Ram suya on the grill at Mallam Garba's, Ojuelegba.

children.text: The winner

Mallam Garba's Grill on Ojuelegba Road scored 9.4, the highest of any spot by a clear margin. The meat is sliced paper-thin, the char is even, and the yaji, ground fresh each afternoon from groundnut, ginger, cloves and dried pepper, is the most balanced we tasted. Ram suya costs ₦5,000 for a generous portion. Go after 7pm and expect a short queue. The grill also does the best tsire skewers we tried, at ₦1,000 each.

body.quote: My father taught me one rule: never slice the meat thick to make the portion look bigger. People can tell.
body.cite: Garba Musa, owner, Mallam Garba's Grill

children.text: The rest of the top five
2. Kano Corner, Obalende: 8.9. Superb kidney suya and the hottest yaji in Lagos. ₦3,500.
3. Suya Boy, Lekki Phase 1: 8.6. Cleanest kitchen, excellent chicken. ₦6,000.
4. Alhaji's Tsire, Ikeja: 8.4. Thick, juicy beef with plenty of onion. ₦4,000.
5. Yaba Night Grill: 8.1. Best value on the list, generous portions for ₦2,500.

A few lessons from twenty grills. Price had almost no link to quality: the most expensive spot we tried came fifteenth. Freshly ground yaji makes more difference than anything else, and most of the low scorers were using powder that tasted stale. And the best suya is almost always from the grill with the longest queue of motorbikes parked outside, not cars. Ram, where you can get it, was richer and more forgiving than beef, and kidney divided the panel completely: two loved it, three refused a second piece. Our panel's final advice: eat it hot, on the spot, out of the newspaper it comes in. Suya that has travelled forty minutes in a car is a different, sadder dish.

title: Recipe: coconut jollof for a Sunday crowd
excerpt: Coconut milk instead of stock, a proper smoky bottom, and enough to feed ten without stress.

children.text: Every family has a jollof rule. In mine it is that the pot must be big enough for whoever turns up. This version, cooked in coconut milk, is rich, slightly sweet and forgiving, which makes it ideal for a crowd. It serves ten generously and takes about an hour and a quarter.

body.caption: Coconut jollof, straight from the pot, with fried plantain.
body.alt: Coconut jollof, straight from the pot, with fried plantain.

children.text: Ingredients
1.5kg long-grain parboiled rice, washed until the water runs clear
6 large plum tomatoes
4 red bell peppers (tatashe)
3 scotch bonnet peppers
3 large onions
4 tablespoons tomato paste
250ml vegetable oil
2 x 400ml tins coconut milk, or the milk of 2 fresh coconuts
750ml chicken stock or water
2 teaspoons curry powder, 2 teaspoons dried thyme, 3 bay leaves
4 stock cubes and salt to taste
Method
1. Blend the tomatoes, bell peppers, scotch bonnets and two onions until smooth. Boil in a dry pot for 15 minutes to reduce.
2. Slice the last onion. Heat the oil in your biggest pot and fry the onion until soft. Add the tomato paste and fry for 5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens.
3. Add the reduced pepper base, curry, thyme, bay and stock cubes. Fry for 15 minutes, until the oil rises to the top.
4. Add the coconut milk and stock, bring to the boil and taste: it should be slightly too salty.
5. Stir in the rice, cover with foil and then the lid, and cook on the lowest heat for 30 to 35 minutes. Do not stir.
6. When the rice is tender, turn up the heat for 3 minutes to char the bottom. Rest for 10 minutes, then fork through and serve.

body.quote: The bottom of the pot is not burnt. It is the best part, and the cook gets it first.

children.text: Serve with fried plantain, coleslaw and grilled chicken, or with fried fish. Leftovers keep for three days in the fridge and reheat well with a splash of water. All the ingredients cost about ₦32,000 in Lagos this month, which works out at just over ₦3,000 a plate. If you are cooking on gas, a heat diffuser under the pot stops the bottom burning before the top is cooked.

title: The Port Harcourt fishmonger every chef calls first
excerpt: Before dawn at the Creek Road waterfront, Ibiso Tamuno decides what half the city's best kitchens will cook that night.

children.text: It is 4:30am at the waterfront near Creek Road market in Port Harcourt, and Ibiso Tamuno is already arguing. Politely, but firmly, with a fisherman who wants ₦3,000 more for a basket of croaker than she thinks it is worth. She wins. She usually does. By sunrise, the fish will be on ice and on its way to the kitchens of half the restaurants we love in the city.

body.caption: Ibiso Tamuno checking the morning catch at the Creek Road waterfront.
body.alt: Ibiso Tamuno checking the morning catch at the Creek Road waterfront.

children.text: Thirty years on the water

Tamuno has sold fish for thirty years, starting at fourteen beside her mother. Today she runs a small business with four employees, two motorbikes with cool boxes and a single, very full phone. Her customers include Tide Table, Ofo Lounge, Mama Ibiere's Fish Spot and a dozen hotels, and they all say the same thing: she tells you the truth about what is good today, even if it means selling you less.

body.quote: If the fish is not fresh, I will not sell it to a chef. My name goes on that plate, even if nobody knows it.

children.text: Her method is simple. She knows which boats come in from where and which fishermen ice their catch properly. She looks at the eyes, presses the flesh and smells the gills of every fish she buys. And she refuses anything that has spent too long in the sun, which on a hot morning can mean turning away a third of what she is offered. Her advice for home cooks is just as direct.
Croaker: the all-rounder, for grilling, frying or pepper soup
Catfish: best alive, for point-and-kill pepper soup
Barracuda: firm and meaty, ideal on a charcoal grill
Periwinkle and clams: buy only if they close when tapped
Best day to buy: Tuesday, after the weekend boats return

You can buy from her directly at the waterfront before 7am, or ask the chefs at any of the places above where their fish came from. They will tell you, and they will probably smile. Bring a cool box, cash and a willingness to be told no. She will not sell you anything she would not cook for her own family.

title: About EKPO
lede: EKPO tells the stories of the people shaping Nigerian style and culture. We document the designers, artists, musicians and cooks building something new, and we make their work easy to find.
description: EKPO tells the stories of the people shaping Nigerian style and culture.
quote: Ekpo is a masquerade of the Ibibio and Efik people: a spirit that comes out in costume to tell the community something true.

children.text: We started EKPO in Lagos because the most exciting fashion in the world was being made a few streets from our office, and almost nobody was writing it down properly.

Today we publish every day across ten sections, from Fashion and Editorials to Ekpo Eats. We make our own shoots and films, print a quarterly magazine, and once a year bring sixty Nigerian brands together at EKPO Market.
We are independent. We are funded by readers who buy our print issues and products, and by partners who advertise with us. Paid partnerships are always labelled.
